guides.title: Found an injured bird
guides.summary: Who to call first, how to catch, contain and transport an injured bird, and why food, water and heat can kill it.

chunks.heading: Injured birds and other wildlife
chunks.text: _How to help an injured bird or wild animal in New York City, and the things that quietly make it worse._

chunks.heading: Who to call right now
chunks.text:
Put the animal in a cardboard box with small air holes, somewhere dark and quiet, and do not give it food or water. Then:

- **Injured bird or small mammal, any borough:** [The Wild Bird Fund](/org/the-wild-bird-fund), 565 Columbus Ave, Manhattan. Walk in any day 9am–7pm, no appointment. (646) 306-2862.
- **Cannot get there:** email the NYC Bird Alliance injured-bird volunteers at injuredbird@nycbirdalliance.org with your exact location and phone number. The reply is automatic and carries instructions; read them.
- **Hawk, owl or other large bird:** do not approach it. Email the same NYC Bird Alliance address, or call 311 and ask for the Urban Park Rangers. The region's raptor rehabilitator is [WINORR](/org/winorr-wildlife-in-need-of-rescue-and-rehabilitation).
- **Wild baby cottontail, or a fox, raccoon or other mammal:** [Cottontail Cottage](/org/cottontail-cottage-wildlife-rehab), (914) 933-7559, any hour. Or find the nearest licensed rehabilitator in the [DEC directory](/org/nys-dec-find-a-wildlife-rehabilitator); the DEC line is (844) 332-3267.
- **Also in the city:** [Wildlife Freedom Foundation](/org/wildlife-freedom-foundation), a licensed rehabilitator on Roosevelt Island, by email.
- **Seal, whale, dolphin or sea turtle on a beach:** keep your distance and call [the stranding hotline](/org/ny-marine-mammal-and-sea-turtle-stranding-hotline), (631) 369-9829.

chunks.heading: If a cat may have touched it
chunks.text: If a bird or small mammal is attacked by a cat, it is an emergency. Cats have an anaerobic bacterium called Pasteurella in their saliva which is deadly. If an animal attacked by a cat does not get the proper antibiotic in a short time (usually within the day) it is likely fatal. Please also note that very often a cat bite will leave NO visible wounds, even if the teeth have punctured the skin. Even more reason to get to a rehabber immediately! If cats are in the area where you find an injured bird, assume it may have been bitten, and get to a rehabber immediately.

If you see a bird hit a window, then it needs to be transported to a rehabber. If a window strike is not fatal upon impact, it leaves a bird in shock, and it needs to be treated by a rehabber. Many times people will leave the bird and say it flew away a few minutes later-this is a shock response, and sadly most of these birds will die later. So if you see a bird hit a window, contain it and get it to a rehabber. You can also prevent window collisions by using Feather Friendly, or other products in a variety of price ranges. More info at https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/why-birds-hit-windows-and-how-you-can-help-prevent-it/#

In urban areas with limited green space, we're more likely to see baby birds going through the natural process of fledgling or leaving the nest.

In most cases, these birds do not need your help! Even though the bird may look helpless, it's probably okay and you should leave the young bird alone. Often people pick up perfectly healthy fledglings because they see a bird on the ground, unable to fly, and looking rough. It’s likely it’s a normal part of a birds life! Part of a bird becoming an adult is them learning how to fly, while the parents are hidden nearby and watching, looking for food, and letting their baby learn independence. This can take a few days, or a few weeks. If the bird can stand and hop, leave it alone. This image shows a lot of common fledglings https://www.wildbirdfund.org/how-to-help/rescue/field-guide-to-fledglings/

This article explains the stages of bird development, and when to help, and not help-

<https://www.audubon.org/news/when-you-should-and-should-not-rescue-baby-birds>

<https://chirpforbirds.com/how-to/what-to-do-wh

chunks.heading: How to handle injured birds
chunks.text:
Approach the bird slowly and quietly from behind, pointed away from traffic, so as to not scare it. Do not talk to the bird as you walk toward it. Wild birds are frightened of humans and will try to escape, often flying back into glass or into the street. Even a soft and gentle voice is stressful. If you see a bird that has been injured, capture it as soon as possible-they often fly away in shock after a few minutes only to die later, so the sooner you can get them, the better chance they have to survive.

The best way to catch a bird is to corner and either scoop up like a burrito or soft football, or toss a sheet or something similar over them, and then scoop up. Gently but firmly grab the bird by putting one or two hands over its wings. Avoid uneven grips or pushing the wings in any direction, this can cause or worsen internal injuries.

Put the bird into a cardboard box with holed poked into it for air (a few pencil sized holes are more than enough, you don’t want them to be too big as birds bodies are much smaller than we see from the outside). Close up the box securely so the bird doesn’t escape. Just because they can fly, doesn’t mean they’re not injured, they may be in shock.

Never touch a bird after touching a cat. Wash your hands between animals. There are few diseases communicable from birds to humans, make sure you wash your hands after handling any animal.

Regarding baby birds (especially those that are close to naked or are in distress for some reason) and need transport to WBF. These babies are very fragile and vulnerable to cold and exposure to cold. They usually need supplemental heat of some kind (the sock with rice or ziplock bag with water (warmed up in the microwave) can work well as well as a heating pad on low while bird is at a house anyway. Th

chunks.heading: Where to take injured wildlife
chunks.text:
A licensed rehabber is registered with the state and federal government. The training for and maintenance of licensing is extensive. Many well intentioned people claim to care for and rescue wildlife, but only a licensed rehabber is legally, technically, and ethically qualified to care for wildlife. The process of assessment, care, and recovery requires specialized knowledge and equipment, and cannot be replicated at home.

Please note, a vet or tech that cares for domestic animals may not be trained, equipped, or licensed to care for wild animals-even domestic birds are very different from wild birds. It’s always best to to go a rehabber.

If you find an injured or sick bird, get it into a cardboard box with small airholes, and take it to the Wild Bird Fund. They are open every day from 9am-7pm, and you do not need an appointment-just go to their facility!

<https://www.wildbirdfund.org>

Keep it in a dark and quiet room to minimize stress and stimuli. If you are unable to go, you can also contact NYC Bird Alliance Injured Bird response team (citywide network of volunteers specializing in care and transport of injured birds).

Email injuredbird@nycbirdalliance.org and someone will reply shortly. The email hotline is monitored by volunteers all day. When you compose the email, you will notice that it’s automatically populates with instructions-please read and follow them. It’s important to give your exact location and phone number so someone can help you faster. Please note these are all volunteers, just like us, their capacity may be limited, so please be kind and understanding.

There are more tips at-

<https://nycbirdalliance.org/take-action/help-a-bird-in-trouble/what-to-do-if-you-find-an-injured-bird>

chunks.heading: Why not to feed injured wildlife
chunks.text:
Giving any injured or sick bird (or any wildlife) food or water is never ok. This is for a few reasons.

- A compromised bird may be dehydrated, cold, or managing internal injuries. Every last bit of energy they have is being used to maintain critical body functions. It takes a lot of energy to digest food, energy that they do not have enough of. Diverting that limited energy to something non critical, like digesting food and water, will cause organ failure or death.
- There may also be internal injures that we don’t see, or delayed onset symptoms. A bird ingesting water in a compromised state can aspirate or drown, and the ingestion of the food itself can exacerbate internal damage. The severity of the situation may not be apparent immediately, especially to the untrained eye, so it’s best not to introduce food or water until a professional assessment has been made.
- When a bird is physically injured, it is also in diminished mental capacity, such as stress or shock. They are not in a coherent mental state, and can’t make the right decision to abstain from food or water, so it’s best not to offer any to them.
- An emaciated bird cannot process solid food, and needs a rehabber to evaluate specific circumstances before introducing nutrition
- Wildlife also has very specific nutritional needs, especially when injured (yes, even pigeons!) Licensed rehabbers go through extensive training and work with scientists to ensure this nutritional knowledge is current. The products they use are not the same as used for pets, many are not even commercially available. When the bird is well enough to eat, they will be fed many nutritious, species appropriate meals.
- the other danger of improper feeding is imprinting. Imprinting refers to when an animal forms attachments to other livi

chunks.heading: Why is some wildlife euthanized
chunks.text: It can be heartbreaking to go through the trouble of rescuing wildlife and taking to a rehabber, only to find out the animal was euthanized. For many, the instinct is often to blame the rehabber-how can someone end the life of an animal? However, this decision is not made lightly-every other option is considered before this, and euthanasia is a last resort. If an animal is not responding to treatment, has injuries or illness too severe for treatment, or is in a condition where their quality of life will not be good after treatment (such as excessive pain and suffering) a rehabber may decide humane euthanasia is the appropriate next step. As devastating as the ending of a life may be, it is cruel to force an animal to live through excessive suffering. Wildlife can suffer in ways that aren’t always apparent to the untrained eye-I’ve counseled many well meaning people who have kept a wild animal in domestic care, without realizing the animal is dying an extended death. The same emotions and attachments that drive our passion to help animals can also cloud our judgment, and a logical decision is not always the most pleasant one. Please remember-nobody wants to euthanize an animal, and rehabbers, like rescuers, are driven by care and love. There is a vast emotional toll on the folks who have to do this extremely difficult job, and our compassion should extend to them too.

guides.title: Save an animal from the shelter’s at-risk list
guides.summary: How to get an at-risk animal out of the city shelter, who can actually pull it, and what to say.

chunks.heading: Save an animal from the shelter’s at-risk list
chunks.text:
_How to get an at-risk animal out of the city shelter, who can actually pull it, and what to say._

New York City's public animal shelter is Animal Care Centers of NYC (ACC). When an animal there urgently needs to leave, ACC puts it on an “at-risk list”. Many of these animals cannot be adopted directly by a member of the public. They can only leave through an approved rescue group, which ACC calls a “New Hope partner”.

So if you want to save a particular at-risk animal, you usually cannot do it on your own. You need a New Hope partner to take the animal, with you lined up as the foster or adopter. This page is about reaching those partners fast.

chunks.heading: HOW MUCH TIME YOU HAVE
chunks.text:
ACC posts the at-risk list three times a week, on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday evenings at 6:00 PM. Each posting stays viewable for 42 hours, until 12:00 noon two days later: Sunday's list closes Tuesday noon, Tuesday's closes Thursday noon, Thursday's closes Saturday noon. Act before the listing closes.

ACC states that being on the at-risk list does not mean an animal is automatically euthanised. Euthanasia happens only when no placement has been secured. The reason to act fast is to secure that placement while the animal is still listed.

chunks.heading: DO THIS NOW, IN ORDER
chunks.text:
- Confirm the animal is still listed. Find it on ACC's live at-risk list, linked below, and note its name and A-number. The list also shows whether it is already reserved.
- Submit ACC's pre-screener, linked below. This tells ACC you have a home, and ACC forwards your details to rescue partners. Do this even though you are also doing the next step. Note that the pre-screener is a Google form and asks you to sign in with a Google account; if you do not have one to hand, go straight to contacting partners and come back to it.
- Contact partners yourself, at the same time. Using the list below, contact every partner that takes your animal's species, through every channel each one lists, in parallel. Do not wait for one reply before trying the next, and do not assume a phone call is faster than a form or an email. Use the wording below so you are not composing a message under pressure.
- Keep going until a partner confirms the pull with ACC. A promising reply is not a pull. The partner has to notify ACC and complete their paperwork to take the animal. Only stop once that is confirmed.

chunks.heading: OFFICIAL ACC LINKS
chunks.text:
- Live at-risk list, cats and dogs, updated Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday at 6 PM - https://newhope.shelterbuddy.com/Animal/List
- ACC's pre-screener, to submit if you have a home ready - https://forms.gle/ozHex3uqvNkQt2dq9 - needs a Google sign-in.
- ACC's emergency placement page, which carries the list and the form together - https://nycacc.org/emergency-placement/
- ACC's full official list of all registered New Hope partners, around 250 of them - https://nycacc.org/programs/new-hope-partners/
- What the New Hope programme is, in ACC's own words - https://nycacc.org/programs/new-hope/
- Outcomes for animals that were previously listed - https://nycacc.org/adoption/at-risk-outcomes/

chunks.heading: WHAT TO SAY
chunks.text:
Fill in the brackets. The committed-home line is the one that gets a yes.

By phone, or as a voicemail: Hi, I'm calling about an at-risk animal at ACC. Name [ ], A-number [ ], at the [borough] centre, listed until [deadline]. [I am / I have] a committed foster or adopter ready the moment the animal is pulled. Can your organisation pull it as a New Hope partner? I'll complete any application right away and arrange transport. Please call or text me back at [your number].

By email, subject line: Urgent at-risk animal, committed home ready - A-number [ ], listed until [deadline]

By email, body: Name [ ], A-number [ ], [borough] centre, listed until [deadline]. [I am / There is] a committed foster or adopter ready the moment the animal is pulled. Can your organisation pull it as a New Hope partner? I'll complete any application immediately and arrange transport. Reach me at [phone] or [email].

Through an online form, kept short because forms cap the length: At-risk animal, A-number [ ], [borough] centre, listed until [deadline]. [I am / I have] a committed foster or adopter ready now. Can you pull it as a New Hope partner? I'll complete your application and arrange transport immediately. Contact: [phone] / [email].

chunks.heading: WHO TO CONTACT
chunks.text: Contact every organisation that takes your animal's species, through every channel it lists, at the same time. This is a working list of ACC New Hope partners across the New York, New Jersey and Connecticut area, not every ACC partner; ACC's complete official list is linked above. Where an organisation has its own entry in this directory, that entry is where its contact details are kept current.

guides.title: Reporting animal abuse or neglect
guides.summary: Who to call in New York City, what to write down, and why it is the police rather than the ASPCA.

chunks.heading: Reporting animal abuse or neglect
chunks.text:
_Who to call in New York City, what to write down, and why it is the police rather than the ASPCA._

Since 2014 the NYPD, not the ASPCA, leads all animal cruelty response in New York City. When you call 311 or 911 your report goes to the police. Calling the ASPCA to report cruelty will send you back to 311.

The ASPCA still works behind the scenes - forensic exams, medical care, housing for victims, and support to prosecutors - but it is not who you call first.

chunks.heading: IS THIS HAPPENING RIGHT NOW?
chunks.text:
- Call 911 if an animal or a person is in immediate danger, or a crime is in progress: an animal being beaten, a dogfight, an animal left in a hot or freezing car, an attack. 911 is also correct any time a person is also at risk.
- Call 311, or report online at portal.311.nyc.gov, for ongoing abuse or neglect that is NOT an active emergency: a chained dog with no shelter, repeated cruelty, a hoarding situation, an animal denied food, water or vet care. 311 routes your report to the NYPD precinct that covers that location.

chunks.heading: HOW TO REPORT SO IT ACTUALLY GETS ACTED ON
chunks.text:
- Report while it is happening if you safely can. The sooner you report, the more likely police can locate the animal and the person, and see the conditions themselves. Delay is the single biggest reason reports go nowhere.
- Give the exact location and specifics: address or cross streets, a description of the animal, a description of the person, and what you saw. You do not have to prove cruelty, only reasonably suspect it. Reporting in good faith is protected.
- Document before, or alongside, reporting. Photos, video, dates and times, and a written note of what you witnessed each time. A report backed by dated evidence is far harder to close without action.
- You can report anonymously. 311 and Crime Stoppers both take anonymous reports. Giving your contact details is optional but helps investigators follow up and can matter for prosecution. Choose based on your safety.
- Expect it to be slow, and keep a record. The NYPD does not share details of open investigations, so you often will not see what happens. That does not mean nothing did. If abuse continues, report again with your new dated observations; a pattern strengthens the case.

chunks.heading: WHAT TO WRITE DOWN - capture this for every incident
chunks.text:
- Date and time you witnessed it.
- Exact location: address or nearest cross streets.
- The animal: species, breed if known, colour, size, condition.
- The person: description, and their relationship to the animal if known.
- What you saw, in plain factual terms: what was done, or what was missing (food, water, shelter, vet care).
- How many times you have seen it.
- Photos or video if you can capture them safely, without trespassing or confronting anyone.
- Names of any other witnesses.

chunks.heading: WHO TO CONTACT
chunks.text:
- NYC 311 - 311 - portal.311.nyc.gov - ongoing abuse or neglect, non-emergency; routes to your NYPD precinct. The online report lets you upload photos, video and documents. Takes anonymous reports.
- NYPD Crime Stoppers - (800) 577-8477 - crimestoppers.nypdonline.org - anonymous tip on ongoing abuse, fighting, or a specific location. Also reachable as 800-577-TIPS. Fully anonymous tip line and online form.
- Your local NYPD precinct - nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/find-your-precinct.page - report in-progress cruelty directly and ask for the ASPCA Liaison Officer. If a precinct says it has none, ask for the Neighborhood Coordination Officer or the Community Affairs Officer and say you want to file an animal abuse complaint. Not anonymous.
- HSUS dogfighting tip line - (877) 847-4787 - humaneworld.org - suspected organised dogfighting that is not in progress. Also reachable as 877-TIP-HSUS. Reward up to $5,000 for a tip leading to a conviction. For fighting in progress call 911. Takes anonymous reports.
- ASPCA Community Engagement - for a struggling owner who needs help with food, vet care or supplies rather than punishment. Agencies and the public can refer, by email to referrals@aspca.org. Helps keep pets with their owners when the problem is hardship, not cruelty.

chunks.heading: IF PEOPLE ARE AT RISK TOO
chunks.text:
Animal abuse often occurs alongside domestic violence, child abuse and elder abuse. If you are afraid for your own safety or someone else's, or an abuser is using a pet to threaten or control you, use these lines. Many domestic violence shelters can now keep pets safe too, so fear of leaving an animal behind does not have to trap someone. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

- NYC Domestic Violence Hotline - (800) 621-4673 - nyc.gov/content/endgbv/pages/hotlines - abuse of a person alongside a pet, safety planning, leaving safely. Also reachable as 800-621-HOPE. 24/7, confidential, multilingual. Takes anonymous calls.
- URI PALS - (646) 588-0030 - urinyc.org/uripals - for a survivor who needs to leave but cannot abandon a pet. A New York City shelter programme that houses survivors together with their pets: dogs, cats and small animals.
- Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (988) - 988 - 988lifeline.org - if you or someone else needs mental health or crisis support. Free, confidential, multilingual, 24/7. New York City routes its mental health crisis line through 988. Takes anonymous calls.
- ASPCA Animal Poison Control - (888) 426-4435 - aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control - if an animal has been poisoned or exposed to a toxin. Staffed 24/7, 365 days a year.

This is for MEDICAL emergencies, not rescue/adoption. If a cat is hit by a car, bleeding, not breathing, seizing, can't urinate, collapsed, or ate something toxic: go to a 24hr ER now. Call ahead so they're ready.

- Park Slope Veterinary Center - 639 4th Ave 11232 - (718) 369-7387 - discounted feral s/n for Certified TNR Caretakers.
- Faithful Friends Animal Hospital - 2455 McDonald Ave 11223 - (718) 339-7387 - discounted feral s/n for Certified TNR Caretakers.

chunks.heading: MANHATTAN - feral-friendly / low-cost clinics

chunks.heading: BRONX - feral-friendly / low-cost clinics
chunks.text:

- Also usable: HSNY (Manhattan) and the citywide certificate/coupon programs.

chunks.heading: STATEN ISLAND - feral-friendly / low-cost clinics
chunks.text:
- SICAW Certificate Program - low-cost s/n certificates w/ partner SI vets (under half normal price); apply at sicawsaves.org/resources.
- Island Bird Cat & Dog Vet Group - 375 Manor Rd 10314 - (718) 370-9472 - feral-friendly (Bideawee list).
- P.L.U.T.O. Rescue - runs a low-cost s/n program (see Staten Island rescues).
- Toby stationary clinic (Brooklyn) serves SI community cats - (347) 816-2899.

chunks.heading: DENTALS FOR FERAL / UNHANDLEABLE CATS (bigger than a s/n - needs a feral-experienced clinic, done under sedation in the trap)
chunks.text:
- Park Slope Veterinary Center - 639 4th Ave, Bklyn 11232 - (718) 369-7387 - BEST lead: feral-friendly + Dr. Szacki's practice explicitly does dental work (cleanings/extractions) and works with TNR caretakers.
- BBAWC Rescue Clinic - 76 Montague St 11201 - (917) 426-3335 - feral-friendly, does sedated exams/basic care; ask if the dental is in scope or a referral.
- Faithful Friends (2455 McDonald Ave, Bklyn - (718) 339-7387) + Animal General (558 Columbus Ave, Man - (212) 501-9600) - feral-friendly list; call to confirm they'll do a dental on an unhandleable cat.
- Long Island Animal Surgery (Patchogue/Glen Cove) - advertises low-cost dental cleanings/surgeries for FERAL cats, no extra handling charge - worth the trip for a bigger dental.
- HOW TO ASK: 'This is a feral/unhandleable cat needing a dental - can you sedate in the trap and do the dental assessment + extractions under that same anesthesia?' Confirm scope, bloodwork, and cost BEFORE trapping. A dental is bigger than a s/n, so use a full-service feral-friendly clinic, not a high-volume s/n clinic.

chunks.heading: HELP PAYING VET BILLS (financial aid - prevents economic euthanasia; apply to several at once, funds go to the vet)
chunks.text:
- NYSAVE - NYC-specific EMERGENCY funding for low-income NYC residents whose cat/dog needs urgent care they can't afford. Your vet applies on your behalf - ask the treating clinic to contact NYSAVE right away. (via Mayor's Alliance / animalalliancenyc.org/need-help/vetcare).
- AMC 'Charlie's Fund' (Animal Medical Center, Manhattan) - free/subsidized emergency care; pet must first be seen by an AMC vet, apply within 5 business days of treatment start. amcny.org/financial-assistance.
- RedRover Relief - urgent-care grants (often 24-48hr); redrover.org. The Pet Fund - non-urgent/chronic care. Frankie's Friends - lifesaving emergency/specialty. For The Love of Alex - urgent cat/dog care.
- Condition-specific: cancer (Live Like Roo, Magic Bullet, Riedel & Cody), chronic/specialty (The Pet Fund, Pet Lifeline). CareCredit + Scratchpay = medical payment plans many NYC clinics accept.
- HOW: get a written itemized estimate from the vet + proof of need (SNAP/Medicaid/income), then apply to MULTIPLE programs at once (funding is limited and runs out).

chunks.heading: OWNER-SUPPORT / SURRENDER PREVENTION (keep a cat in its home - ACC prevented 3,813 surrenders in one year)
chunks.text:
Note: this tab is a quick-reference layer; the same clinics/orgs also appear (with fuller detail) in the main sheet's 'Clinics' section and borough sections. Feral cats MUST go to a feral-experienced clinic in a covered trap.

- ACC CommunityPets - CommunityPets@nycacc.org - free/reduced vet referrals, deferred intake, help during hospitalization/DV/eviction; the surrender-avoidance line. ACC runs a PET FOOD PANTRY at its Bronx Resource Center (email for location/hours).
- ASPCA + Food Bank For NYC partnership - free pet food distributed through 250+ Food Bank partner pantries in ALL 5 boroughs; recipients also get access to ASPCA affordable vet care/spay-neuter. Find a pantry via foodbanknyc.org or City Harvest's food-locator map (cityharvest.org).
- PAWS NY - paws.nyc.org - pet food pantry + low-income vet care + in-home help (litter, feeding, walking) for low-income NYers with impaired mobility (age/illness/disability).
- NEW (2026): the city budget funds pop-up PET FOOD PANTRIES + spay/neuter in every borough via community partners - check your City Council Member's office or DOHMH for current locations.
- Feeding Pets of the Homeless (petsofthehomeless.org) - pet food via partner pantries/soup kitchens/shelters for people who are homeless or in crisis.
- Local rescues that point to pantry days: Bronx Community Cats, ARQ (Queens), MeowRoof (Queens), Loving Touch, Mama Chris (SI) - or ask 311 for the nearest current one.
- RescueNYC - holding/recovery space so a caretaker isn't forced to surrender during a TNR or medical situation.

guides.title: Community cats, colonies and starting TNR
guides.summary: How trap-neuter-return works in New York City, and who will help you do it.

chunks.heading: Community cats, colonies and starting TNR
chunks.text:
_How trap-neuter-return works in New York City, and who will help you do it._

> COLONY & FERAL CAT CARE - managing an outdoor community-cat colony end to end

A community cat is an outdoor cat without a direct owner. Some are friendly (may be adoptable), most ferals are not - TNR + lifelong colony care is the humane, effective path. Verified vs Bideawee/FCI, Neighborhood Cats, NYC MOAW, Urban Cat League, 2026-08-26.

chunks.heading: STEP 1 - GET TNR-CERTIFIED (free; unlocks free s/n, trap loans, transport)
chunks.text:
- Neighborhood Cats TNR Certification Workshop - monthly online, certifies you as a Certified TNR Caretaker. neighborhoodcats.org/how-to-tnr. 15,000+ New Yorkers certified.
- NYC Feral Cat Initiative (Bideawee) - also runs certification + colony-care workshops + a 7-day helpdesk (nycfci.happyfox.com/new).
- Certification is what makes the free/low-cost s/n, trap banks, and transport (all on 'Clinics, traps & support') available to you.

chunks.heading: STEP 2 - REGISTER THE COLONY (protects it + tracks progress)
chunks.text:
- Cat Stats colony registry (Neighborhood Cats / Mayor's Alliance) - catstats.org/nyc - log your colony, cats, and s/n status.
- Registration helps document TNR progress, coordinate with other caretakers, and can protect a colony's feeding site.

chunks.heading: STEP 3 - TRAP & FIX (see 'Clinics, traps & support' for trap banks + free/low-cost s/n)
chunks.text:
- Borrow traps: Neighborhood Cats, ASPCA, FCI, Muffin's (details on the clinics tab).
- Free/low-cost s/n for community cats: Toby Project (all 5 boroughs, free), ASPCA, plus feral-friendly clinics by borough.
- An EAR-TIP (left ear, squared off) = already spayed/neutered + rabies-vaccinated. Don't re-trap ear-tipped cats.

chunks.heading: STEP 4 - ONGOING COLONY CARE
chunks.text:
- Winter shelters: Urban Cat League + FCI have build guides/workshops (insulated, straw-not-blankets, small entrance).
- Food/water + discreet feeding stations that don't create odor/waste nuisance (keeps neighbors + the colony safe).
- Colony-support groups that help caretakers directly (with contacts): Bronx Community Cats (bronxcommunitycats.org), ARQ/Queens (arqadopt.org), MeowRoof/Queens (meowroof.org), Ocean Hill Cats/Bklyn (info@oceanhillcats.com), Good Home/Bklyn trap bank (info@goodhomepetadoptions.org), Mama Chris/SI (text 347-983-2240).

chunks.heading: FRIENDLY CATS / KITTENS FOUND IN A COLONY (pull for adoption)
chunks.text:
- Socialize: Urban Cat League Taming Toolkit (see 'Lost-found & behavior' tab). Under 8 wks socialize easily; older takes longer.
- Neonatal/bottle-babies too young to survive outdoors: route to a nursery - Itty Bitty City Kitties, Cats of Meow York, Bay Ridge Kittens, Kittens and Barbells (see Specialty view).

chunks.heading: WHEN A CAT CAN'T BE RETURNED (site lost, unsafe, or truly unadoptable feral)
chunks.text:
- Working-cat / barn relocation: Urban Cat League, MeowSquad, For Animals Inc. place un-adoptable ferals as working cats (barns, warehouses, breweries).
- Hard Hat Cats - places working/feral cats at NYC businesses (has placed inside the Brooklyn Navy Yard) - hardhatcats@gmail.com.

chunks.heading: FERAL MEDICAL / EMERGENCIES
chunks.text:
- Sick/injured feral: the feral-friendly clinics on 'Clinics, traps & support' + emergency hospitals on 'Emergency & poison control' (call ahead, bring in a covered trap).
- Feral dentals: see the dental subsection on the clinics tab (Park Slope Vet Center is the best lead).
- Scratched or bitten by a feral? Contact a doctor immediately + report to NYC Health Animal Bite Unit (311). Handle only in a trap/transfer cage.
- KEY CONTACTS (all verified in the main sheet): FCI helpdesk nycfci.happyfox.com/new / (212) 330-0033 - Neighborhood Cats help@neighborhoodcats.org / (212) 662-5761 - these two are the backbone for any colony question.

chunks.heading: SERVICES AVAILABLE FOR COLONY / COMMUNITY CATS (what you can actually GET, and who provides it)
chunks.text: Most free services require you to be a Certified TNR Caretaker (free to become - see Step 1). Register with the provider first.

chunks.heading: SPAY/NEUTER + RABIES + EAR-TIP (the core service, FREE for certified caretakers):
chunks.text: - Toby Project: FREE, all 5 boroughs ($5 rabies only). ASPCA: FREE via RSS (aspcapro.org/scheduler). HSNY: low-cost. NSALA feral package $40 (s/n + rabies + FVRCP + penicillin + eartip). Full list + borough clinics on 'Clinics, traps & support' tab.

chunks.heading: FREE TRANSPORT to/from spay-neuter (if you can't drive traps):
chunks.text: - ASPCA offers free transport to/from its clinics - book with the s/n appointment via RSS. Cats returned to the same pickup spot next day.

chunks.heading: FREE/LOANED TRAPS + drop-traps:
chunks.text: - Neighborhood Cats trap bank (pickup 30 Prince St, Bklyn), ASPCA trap bank (TNRtrapbank@aspca.org), FCI loans, Muffin's rentals. Details on clinics tab.

chunks.heading: FREE CAT FOOD, STRAW & WINTER SHELTERS for colonies:
chunks.text:
- NYC Feral Cat Initiative (FCI) runs periodic giveaways of free cat food, STRAW (best shelter bedding - insulates, wicks moisture), and pre-made winter shelters to Certified TNR Caretakers. Ask the FCI helpdesk about current giveaways.
- Straw (NOT hay, NOT blankets which hold cold/damp) is the correct insulator; FCI + Neighborhood Cats have build guides + sometimes distribute shelters.
- ASPCA + Food Bank pet-food pantries (all boroughs) can also supply colony feeding (see clinics tab owner-support).

chunks.heading: FREE POSTING OF ADOPTABLE COLONY CATS (friendlies/kittens pulled from the colony):
chunks.text: - FCI posts Certified TNR Caretakers' adoptable cats on its Petfinder page. Borough rescues (see main sheet) also take friendlies into their adoption pipelines.

chunks.heading: GRANTS / FINANCIAL HELP for TNR + colony vet costs:
chunks.text: - FCI has administered ASPCA + In Defense of Animals grants for individuals' TNR/adoption expenses - ask the helpdesk what's currently open. Vet-bill aid (NYSAVE etc.) on clinics tab.

chunks.heading: MEDICAL for colony cats (sick/injured/dental):
chunks.text: - Feral-friendly clinics + emergency hospitals + feral dentals: all on 'Clinics, traps & support' and 'Emergency & poison control' tabs. Trap the cat, bring it covered.

chunks.heading: COMMUNITY-RELATIONS help (neighbor complaints, feeding disputes, moving a feeding station):
chunks.text: - FCI + Neighborhood Cats offer guidance + the 'Love Cats / Hate Cats' outreach materials; Alley Cat Allies has colony-conflict resources. NY State classifies cats (incl. feral) as companion animals - caretaking + feeding is legal, though local feeding rules can vary.

chunks.heading: HANDS-ON HELP (someone to trap with you, holding space, fosters):
chunks.text: - Borough TNR groups that trap alongside you / take friendlies / hold (with contacts): Bronx Community Cats (bronxcommunitycats.org), ARQ (arqadopt.org), MeowRoof (meowroof.org), Ocean Hill Cats (info@oceanhillcats.com), Good Home (info@goodhomepetadoptions.org), Mama Chris SI (text 347-983-2240), Bushwick Street Cats (bushwickstreetcats@gmail.com), North Brooklyn Cats (northbrooklyncats.org/help), Flatbush Cats (help@flatbushcats.org). Match to the colony's neighborhood.
