guides.title: Lost or found a cat
guides.summary: What to do first, where to post, and who helps with searching.

chunks.heading: Lost or found a cat
chunks.text:
_What to do first, where to post, and who helps with searching._

> MICROCHIP, LOST & FOUND, AND BEHAVIOR / SOCIALIZATION HELP

Verified against ACC, Petco Love Lost, 24PetWatch, and Urban Cat League, 2026-08-26.

chunks.heading: LOST A CAT - do all of these fast (80% of lost cats are found within a mile - usually much closer, hiding)
chunks.text:
- Petco Love Lost (petcolove.org/lost) - FREE national database with FACIAL-RECOGNITION photo matching. Upload a clear face photo, report as LOST, print the auto-generated flyer, check every few hours.
- ACC lost/found - nycacc.org/services/lost-and-found - file a Lost Pet Report, search the Found database, and VISIT all open Care Centers in person with a photo + proof of ownership (shelters don't always post daily).
- If chipped: contact the microchip company immediately, report the cat lost, confirm your contact info is current.
- Post to NYC lost-and-found networks: PawBoost, Pet FBI, Nextdoor, Craigslist lost-and-found, and location-based Facebook groups ('Lost and Found Pets of [neighborhood/NYC]'). Make ONE shareable flyer image with photo + last-seen location/time + your number.
- CAT-SPECIFIC SEARCH (cats hide, they don't run far): search silently at DUSK/NIGHT with a flashlight + carrier + smelly food; check under cars, porches, shrubs, basements, alleys, dumpsters. An indoor cat that bolted is usually within a few houses, hiding and silent for days.
- Indoor escape? Search your OWN home first - behind the stove, in cabinets, closets, under furniture. Put their litter box / a worn t-shirt outside the door; the scent can draw them back.
- Ask the people who walk your block: mail carriers, delivery drivers, supers, door attendants, restaurant basement staff, park workers. Post flyers at vets, pet stores, and building mailboxes (get permission on private property).
- Do NOT chase a sighted cat - it makes them bolt. Sit, talk softly, offer food, and consider a humane trap (borrow one - see 'Clinics, traps & support').

chunks.heading: FOUND A CAT
chunks.text:
- Get it SCANNED for a microchip at any vet or shelter (free) - the fastest route to the owner. Also check for a collar/tag and an EAR-TIP (a tipped ear = a TNR'd community cat with a caretaker, not a lost pet - leave it be).
- Report as FOUND on Petco Love Lost + file a found report with ACC. Search local Facebook lost-and-found groups + Nextdoor for a matching 'lost' post.
- SICK or INJURED stray/community cat? Text ACC at (203) 529-5372 or email CommunityPets@nycacc.org - they assess whether it needs help and how. Don't handle an aggressive/fearful cat.
- Healthy, friendly cat? Don't assume it's a stray - it may be an indoor/outdoor neighbor's cat. ACC does NOT accept healthy stray cats; post found flyers + check for a chip first. If truly abandoned, contact a borough rescue.
- NY stray-hold law: found pets generally must be reported to animal control and held a minimum number of days before adoption - check with ACC.

chunks.heading: MICROCHIP REGISTRIES (register the chip - a chip that isn't registered can't reunite anyone)
chunks.text:
- 24PetWatch (24pet.com/products/registry) - North America's largest registry, FREE registration, any chip brand.
- Petco Love Lost - free, doubles as the lost/found database above.
- Don't know the chip company? Look up the number at found.org/owners or the AAHA Universal Lookup (petmicrochiplookup.org).
- Where to GET a cat chipped cheaply: ACC, HSNY, most low-cost clinics on the 'Clinics, traps & support' tab do microchipping at the s/n visit.

chunks.heading: BEHAVIOR / SOCIALIZATION - part A: feral/shy cats & kittens (make them adoptable)
chunks.text:
- Urban Cat League Taming Toolkit (urbancatleague.org/taming-toolkit) - THE NYC resource: written crash-course + 'Taming Feral Kittens & Cats' video + taming blog. Share it with adopters/fosters to prevent back-sliding.
- Rule of thumb: kittens under 8 weeks socialize easily; 8 wks-6 months takes longer but works; adult ferals sometimes too. Work at feeding time when they're hungry, start with head/shoulders, use a large dog crate or a bathroom, hand-feed to build trust.
- UCL workshops: Taming Feral Street Kittens, Bottle-Feeding Neonatals, Building Winter Shelters, Incorporating a 501(c)(3), and the TNR Certification workshop (15,000+ certified).
- Kitten Lady (kittenlady.org) - free how-to videos on neonatal/kitten care + socialization. Cornell Feline Health Center - vet-backed behavior articles.

chunks.heading: BEHAVIOR / SOCIALIZATION - part B: OWNED-cat problems (these are the #1 surrender triggers - solvable!)
chunks.text:
Prevention beats everything: a registered microchip + keeping cats indoors is the single strongest safety net. A loud noise or sudden movement can send an outdoor cat running - think of a cat outside as a toddler alone.

- FREE National Cat Behavior Helpline - email felinehelpline@gmail.com with your contact info + a one-line issue ('cat not using litter box'); free counseling aimed at keeping cats in their homes.
- FIRST STEP for any sudden behavior change (esp. litter box) = a VET VISIT to rule out a medical cause (UTI, kidney, pain). Behavior fixes won't work if it's medical.
- Litter box (10%+ of cats): one box per cat PLUS one extra, scoop daily, unscented clumping litter ~2in deep, big uncovered box, quiet accessible spot. Never punish or place the cat in the box. Spraying (vertical, small amount) is marking, not a box problem - neuter fixes ~90%.
- Cat-to-cat aggression / introductions: separate resources (multiple bowls, beds, boxes, perches), go SLOW with a new cat (scent-swap, then feed on opposite sides of a door, then visual, then supervised). Feliway pheromone diffuser can lower tension. Don't soothe an aroused cat - give space (redirected aggression can turn on you).
- Scratching: it's normal (stretching/marking) - provide tall sturdy posts + horizontal cardboard, don't declaw (harmful; alternatives exist). Reward using the post.
- Authoritative free libraries: ASPCA Common Cat Behavior Issues (aspca.org/pet-care/cat-care), Pam Johnson-Bennett (catbehaviorassociates.com), Best Friends, Cornell Feline Health Center.
- For serious/persistent cases: ask your vet for a referral to a board-certified veterinary behaviorist (Dip ACVB) or Certified Applied Animal Behaviorist (CAAB).

guides.title: Help keeping your cat
guides.summary: Food, vet bills, housing, and temporary care, before surrender becomes the only option.

chunks.heading: Help keeping your cat
chunks.text:
_Food, vet bills, housing, and temporary care, before surrender becomes the only option._

> OWNER SUPPORT & KEEPING YOUR CAT - help before surrender (contacts inline)

Resources for cat owners who need help - food, in-home care, temporary/crisis fostering, vet-bill aid, housing support, and pet insurance. ACC offers many of these directly and can talk through options. Verified against ACC, Mayor's Alliance, NYSAVE, and AMC, 2026-08-28. Confirm current availability, which changes over time.

chunks.heading: ACC OWNER SUPPORT / SURRENDER PREVENTION
chunks.text:
- ACC CommunityPets - CommunityPets@nycacc.org - (212) 788-4000. Free/reduced vet referrals, spay/neuter, deferred/managed intake, and help during a crisis so a cat can stay in its home. Ask about the surrender-prevention questionnaire; a counselor follows up.
- ACC may also provide supplies (food, litter, carriers) and connect owners to other agencies. To rehome a cat yourself (often less stressful for the cat than shelter intake), ask about ACC's 'Rehoming Your Pet' tools.

chunks.heading: PET FOOD PANTRIES (specific programs)
chunks.text:
- ACC Pet Food Pantry - at the ACC Bronx Resource Center; contact for location, hours, eligibility. CommunityPets@nycacc.org - (212) 788-4000.
- PuppyKitty NYC - runs a pet-food bank; 501(c)(3) rescues can request stock, and it distributes to people in need. foodbank@puppykittynyc.org - puppykittynyc.org.
- Animal Relief Fund (ARF) - NYC org providing pet food to people in need. animalrelieffund.org.
- New York Common Pantry - distributes pet food at events (often with the ASPCA), including in the Bronx. nycommonpantry.org - (917) 720-9700.
- Food Bank For New York City - pet food is sometimes available at member pantries (varies by donations). foodbanknyc.org/get-help.
- ASPCA + Food Bank For NYC partnership - free pet food distributed through Food Bank partner pantries citywide.
- Petco Love 'We Are Family' - collects pet food/litter and distributes through human food-pantry partners across the 5 boroughs; ask your local pantry if they participate.
- Prince Chunk Foundation - pet food + short-term assistance for families in crisis. princechunkfoundation.org.
- Kiso's Pet Food Pantry (Brooklyn) - free pet food, focus on senior citizens. facebook.com/Kisos-Pet-Food-Pantry.
- Feeding Pets of the Homeless - free pet food + vet care via partner sites for people who are homeless or at risk. petsofthehomeless.org.
- Food Help NYC (finder.nyc.gov/foodhelp) lists food pantries, some of which stock pet food; the donateNYC Directory (donatenyc.org) has a Pet Care/Food category.
- NEW (2026): the city budget funds pop-up PET FOOD PANTRIES + spay/neuter in every borough via community events - watch ACC + borough-rescue feeds for dates.

chunks.heading: SENIOR / DISABILITY / ILLNESS - in-home pet care
chunks.text:
- PAWS NY - free in-home help (litter changing, feeding, vet-trip coordination) for low-income seniors and people with illness/disability who struggle with daily pet care. Also runs a pet food pantry. pawsny.org - (212) 203-4760.
- CancerCare Pet Assistance & Wellness (PAW) Program - help with pet-care costs for people in active cancer treatment, with a NYC-resident fund. cancercare.org - (800) 813-4673.

chunks.heading: TEMPORARY / CRISIS CARE - hospitalization, rehab, housing transition
chunks.text:
- PAWS NY - Hospital Respite Program for people who are hospitalized or in rehab, plus a Substance Use Recovery Program for those entering inpatient treatment. referrals@pawsny.org - (212) 203-4760 ext. 306.
- ASPCA Community Engagement - may provide free/subsidized short-term boarding during a crisis; ask about eligibility via aspca.org.
- Animal Haven Community Engagement - short-term boarding for pets whose owners face a temporary crisis (hospitalization, housing transition); space is limited. (212) 274-8511 - animalhaven.org.
- RescueNYC - holding/recovery space so a caretaker isn't forced to surrender during a TNR or medical situation (see main sheet).
- ACC - can coordinate options for people entering DHS temporary housing. admissions@nycacc.org - (212) 788-4000.

chunks.heading: DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE PET SAFE-KEEPING (free; stay-together or safe foster)
chunks.text:
- URI PALS (Urban Resource Institute, People and Animals Living Safely) - the largest DV shelter provider in the U.S.; NYC co-living shelters let survivors bring pets, with private pet-friendly areas. Free. urinyc.org (ask about PALS); NYC DV Hotline (24/7): (800) 621-HOPE / (800) 621-4673.
- Safe Haven Program / MAP Foster - networks of foster homes partnered with DV shelters to care for a pet temporarily when the shelter can't take animals, then reunite. Ask a DV caseworker or the NYC DV Hotline (800) 621-4673.
- PAWS NY - assists with emergency fostering for domestic-violence survivors seeking safety. referrals@pawsny.org - (212) 203-4760 ext. 306.
- RedRover Relief Safe Escape - grants help cover pet boarding/care for survivors leaving abuse. redrover.org/domestic.
- Safe Place for Pets (RedRover) - searchable directory of programs by ZIP. safeplaceforpets.org.
- Safe Havens Mapping Project (Animal Welfare Institute) - directory of shelters with on-site pet housing, boarding partnerships, or foster care during a crisis. safehavensmappingproject.com.
- Sheltering Animals & Families Together (SAF-T) - helps DV shelters house pets on-site. alliephillips.com/saf-tprogram.
- SPCA Westchester Pet Safety Program - safe-keeping for pets in DV-affected households (Westchester-adjacent). spcawestchester.org/pet-safety - (914) 941-2896.

chunks.heading: HOSPICE / SENIOR + LIFETIME-CARE placement
chunks.text:
- Tavi & Friends (Brooklyn) - senior + FIV lifetime care; the specialist. 646-872-1533 - adopt@taviandfriends.org.
- Cat Castle NYC (Manhattan) - through-senior (up to ~16 yrs) and hard cases others won't take. (973) 752-7750 - catcastlenyc.org.
- KittyKind (Manhattan) - senior + special-needs placement. adopt@kittykind.org - kittykind.org.
- Lap of Love - in-home hospice and end-of-life veterinary care across NYC. lapoflove.com - (855) 933-5683.
- There is no NYC-only senior-cat sanctuary; the lifetime-care rescues above plus fosters are the route for an unadoptable senior.

chunks.heading: HELP PAYING VET BILLS (financial aid - prevents economic euthanasia; apply to several at once, funds go to the vet)
chunks.text:
- NYSAVE (NY Save Animals in Veterinary Emergency) - NYC-SPECIFIC emergency funding for sick/injured pets of low-income NYC residents (all 5 boroughs). At/below NYC poverty level (about $41,100 for 1 person / $58,700 for a family of 4); must first be denied by CareCredit/Scratchpay; ~$2,000/yr per household, paid to a participating vet. (917) 669-7281 - info@nysave.org - nysave.org.
- AMC (Schwarzman Animal Medical Center, Manhattan) funds - Charlie's Patient Assistance Fund (free/subsidized EMERGENCY care), Buddy Fund (cancer), Cooper Fund (radiation), SAVE (seniors 65+), plus military/adopted-pet discounts. Pet must be seen at AMC; apply within 5 business days of treatment. funds@amcny.org - (212) 838-8100 - amcny.org/financial-assistance.
- ASPCA Animal Hospital (AAH) - low-cost urgent care in NYC for owners with household income at or below $50,000 (bring EBT/SSI/VA/unemployment/TANF proof). aspca.org/nyc.
- RedRover Relief - grants (avg ~$250) toward urgent, life-threatening care; income under $60,000/yr; paid to the vet. redrover.org/relief - (916) 429-2457.
- The Pet Fund - non-urgent/chronic care (e.g. chronic conditions); contact BEFORE applying. info@thepetfund.com - (916) 443-6007.
- Frankie's Friends - lifesaving emergency/specialty care (pet already seen by a vet, good prognosis). frankiesfriends.org/apply-for-assistance-3.
- Waggle - vet-bill crowdfunding; 100% of funds go to the vet. waggle.org.
- Condition-specific (cats): cancer - Live Like Roo (livelikeroo.org), Magic Bullet Fund (themagicbulletfund.org), Riedel & Cody Fund; FIP/retrovirus + chronic - The Pet Fund; Feline Veterinary Emergency Assistance Program (VAS/ISS); Diabetic Cats in Need (insulin help).
- Humane Society of NY - some cases receive full/partial funding via its Animal Emergency Appe

chunks.heading: PET INSURANCE (for planning ahead, not a bill you already have)
chunks.text:
Note: some resources here (ASPCA, PAWS NY, ACC, Pets of the Homeless) also appear on the 'Clinics, traps & support' tab; contacts are repeated here so this tab stands alone.

- Pet insurance reimburses a percentage of FUTURE covered vet costs after you pay the vet; it does NOT cover pre-existing conditions, so it helps most when started while a cat is young and healthy. Compare deductible, reimbursement %, annual limit, and exclusions.
- Trupanion - trupanion.com - (855) 591-3100. Per-condition deductible; can pay the vet directly at participating clinics; 90% reimbursement.
- Healthy Paws - healthypaws.com - (855) 898-8991. Annual deductible, unlimited annual coverage, 70-90% reimbursement; fast claims.
- ASPCA Pet Health Insurance - aspcapetinsurance.com - (866) 204-6764. Customizable; optional wellness add-on; up to 270 days to submit a claim.
- Nationwide - petinsurance.com - (877) 738-7874. Long-standing; some plans cover lost-pet advertising.
- Pets Best - petsbest.com - (877) 738-7237. Direct-vet-pay option.
- Others widely reviewed for 2026: Embrace, Figo, Lemonade, Spot, Pumpkin, Fetch, MetLife. Get 2-3 quotes and read each policy's exclusions before choosing.
- Tip: ask the insurer in writing how they define a pre-existing condition, and whether curable conditions (e.g. an upper-respiratory infection) can be covered later.

guides.title: Help keeping your dog
guides.summary: Support with costs, housing and behaviour, plus how surrender works if you still need it.

chunks.heading: Help keeping your dog
chunks.text:
_Support with costs, housing and behaviour, plus how surrender works if you still need it._

> OWNER SUPPORT & KEEPING YOUR DOG (contacts inline)

Resources for owners who need help caring for a dog - food, in-home care, temporary fostering, behavior help, vet-bill aid, and housing support. ACC offers many of these directly and can talk through options. Verified against ACC, Mayor's Alliance, and Bideawee on 2026-08-27. Confirm current availability, which changes over time.

chunks.heading: ACC OWNER SUPPORT
chunks.text:
What ACC can help with: reduced-fee routine vet care and spay/neuter; funding for emergency vet care; behavior advice and trainer referrals; reduced-fee pet boarding; tenant/landlord dispute help including NYCHA; help for people entering DHS temporary housing; help for military deployment.

To rehome directly: ACC's 'Rehoming Your Pet' page has tools to help find a new home yourself.

- ACC Admissions / Owner Support: email admissions@nycacc.org or call (212) 788-4000; fill out the questionnaire linked at nycacc.org/services/surrender and a counselor contacts you within about 3 days.

chunks.heading: PET FOOD PANTRIES (specific programs)
chunks.text:
Petco Love 'We Are Family' - collects pet food and litter and distributes through human food-pantry partners across the five boroughs; ask your local pantry if they participate.

- ACC Pet Food Pantry - at the ACC Bronx Resource Center; contact for location, hours, and eligibility. CommunityPets@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000.
- PuppyKitty NYC - runs a pet-food bank; 501(c)(3) rescues can request stock, and it distributes to people in need. foodbank@puppykittynyc.org, puppykittynyc.org.
- Animal Relief Fund (ARF) - NYC organization providing pet food to people in need. animalrelieffund.org.
- New York Common Pantry - distributes pet food at events (often with the ASPCA), including in the Bronx. nycommonpantry.org, (917) 720-9700.
- Food Bank For New York City - pet food is sometimes available at its member pantries (varies by donations). foodbanknyc.org; find a pantry at foodbanknyc.org/get-help.
- Prince Chunk Foundation - provides pet food and short-term assistance to families in crisis. princechunkfoundation.org.
- Strong Paws Rescue Community Pet Pantry - periodic food/supply distributions in the Bronx and Westchester. request@strongpawsrescue.org, strongpawsrescue.org/pet-pantry.
- Kiso's Pet Food Pantry (Brooklyn) - free pet food, with a focus on senior citizens. facebook.com/Kisos-Pet-Food-Pantry.
- Pets of the Homeless - free pet food and vet care through partner sites for people who are homeless or at risk. petsofthehomeless.org.
- Food Help NYC - find nearby food pantries (some stock pet food): finder.nyc.gov/foodhelp. The donateNYC Directory lists a Pet Care/Food category: donatenyc.org.

chunks.heading: SENIOR / DISABILITY / ILLNESS - in-home pet care
chunks.text:
- PAWS NY (Pets Are Wonderful Support) - free in-home help (dog walking, feeding, litter, vet-trip coordination) for low-income seniors and people with illness/disability who struggle with daily pet care. Apply at pawsny.org; (212) 203-4760. Case-by-case eligibility.
- CancerCare Pet Assistance & Wellness (PAW) Program - financial help for pet-care costs for people in active cancer treatment, with a dedicated NYC-resident fund. cancercare.org; (800) 813-4673.
- Paws of War - veterinary care for pets of veterans + first responders. pawsofwar.org.

chunks.heading: TEMPORARY / CRISIS CARE - hospitalization, rehab, housing transition, deployment
chunks.text:
- PAWS NY - Hospital Respite Program for people who are hospitalized or in a rehab facility, plus a Substance Use Recovery Program for those entering inpatient treatment. referrals@pawsny.org, (212) 203-4760 ext. 306, pawsny.org.
- ASPCA Community Engagement - may provide free or subsidized short-term boarding during a crisis; ask about eligibility via aspca.org.
- Animal Haven Community Engagement Program - short-term boarding for pets whose owners face a temporary crisis (hospitalization, housing transition); space is limited. (212) 274-8511, animalhaven.org.
- ACC - can coordinate options for people entering DHS temporary housing or facing military deployment. admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000.
- Foster Dogs Inc - Brooklyn nonprofit that helps connect owners in crisis with temporary fostering. fosterdogsnyc.com.

chunks.heading: DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE PET SAFE-KEEPING (free; stay-together or safe foster)
chunks.text:
- URI PALS (Urban Resource Institute, People and Animals Living Safely) - the largest DV shelter provider in the U.S.; its NYC co-living shelters let survivors bring their pets, with private pet-friendly areas and a dog park. Free. urinyc.org (ask about PALS); NYC DV Hotline (24/7): (800) 621-HOPE / (800) 621-4673.
- Safe Haven Program / MAP Foster - networks of foster homes partnered with DV shelters to care for a pet temporarily when the shelter can't take animals, then reunite. Ask a DV caseworker or the NYC DV Hotline (800) 621-4673 to connect you.
- PAWS NY - assists with emergency fostering for domestic-violence survivors seeking safety. referrals@pawsny.org, (212) 203-4760 ext. 306.
- RedRover Relief - Safe Escape grants help cover pet boarding/care for survivors leaving abuse. redrover.org/domestic.
- Safe Place for Pets (RedRover) - searchable directory of programs ready to help survivors and pets, by ZIP. safeplaceforpets.org.
- Safe Havens Mapping Project (Animal Welfare Institute) - directory of shelters with on-site pet housing, boarding partnerships, or foster care during a crisis. safehavensmappingproject.com / awionline.org.
- Sheltering Animals & Families Together (SAF-T) - helps DV shelters house pets on-site; alliephillips.com/saf-tprogram.
- SPCA Westchester Pet Safety Program - safe-keeping for pets in households affected by domestic violence (Westchester-adjacent). spcawestchester.org/pet-safety, (914) 941-2896.

chunks.heading: HOSPICE / FOSPICE + SENIOR-DOG PLACEMENT
chunks.text:
There is no NYC-based senior-dog sanctuary; senior-specialist sanctuaries in nearby states (e.g. Lily's Legacy, Frosted Faces, Young at Heart) are options for those able to travel.

- Rebound Hounds Fospice - lifetime foster homes for senior and terminal-medical dogs, with medical costs covered by the rescue. reboundhounds.org.
- Mr. Bones & Co. - takes senior and complex-medical dogs case-by-case within its individualized-care program. info@mrbonesandco.org, mrbonesandco.org.
- Red Hook Dog Rescue - special-needs and senior dogs (blind, deaf, amputee), foster-based, Brooklyn. harithspi@gmail.com, redhookdogrescue.org.
- Muddy Paws Rescue + Rescue City - foster-based rescues that place seniors and can advise on hospice fostering. muddypawsrescue.org; rescuecity.nyc.
- Lap of Love - in-home hospice and end-of-life veterinary care across NYC. lapoflove.com, (855) 933-5683.

chunks.heading: BEHAVIOR SUPPORT (a common, workable reason owners seek help)
chunks.text:
- ACC Community Pets Program - free dog training (in person or via Zoom/FaceTime) through partner trainers; behavior guides at nycacc.org/services/behavior-resources. Contact: admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000.
- Bideawee + GoodPup - subsidized virtual 1-on-1 training (first week free via links.goodpup.com/shelter/Bideawee10). Bideawee: bideawee.org, (866) 262-8133.
- ASPCA behavior guides: aspca.org/pet-care/dog-care. Find a credentialed trainer at ccpdt.org, or a veterinary behaviorist at dacvb.org.

chunks.heading: VET-BILL FINANCIAL AID
chunks.text:
- ACC may offer funding for emergency vet care; ask Admissions (admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000). Also: RedRover Relief redrover.org / (916) 429-2457, The Pet Fund thepetfund.com, Frankie's Friends frankiesfriends.org, Waggle waggle.org, Brown Dog Foundation browndogfoundation.org.
- CareCredit (carecredit.com) and Scratchpay (scratchpay.com) financing are accepted at most NYC vets.

chunks.heading: HOUSING SUPPORT
chunks.text:
- NYC Animal Welfare - Animals & Housing/Evictions page (nyc.gov/site/animalwelfare/resources/evictions.page): tenant pet-law guide and resources.
- ACC assists with tenant/landlord and NYCHA matters (admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000). Pet-Inclusive Housing Initiative (petsandhousing.org) lists pet-friendly housing resources.
- Free housing legal help: call 311 and ask for tenant legal services, or NYC Housing Court Answers (housingcourtanswers.org, (212) 962-4795).
- ACC accepts emergency-medical and public-safety cases at any time; call (212) 788-4000. For other situations, the options above may help. Availability changes - confirm current programs when you reach out.

guides.title: Low-cost vet care, spay/neuter and dog licensing
guides.summary: Affordable veterinary care across the five boroughs, and how to license a dog in NYC.

chunks.heading: Low-cost vet care, spay/neuter and dog licensing
chunks.text:
_Affordable veterinary care across the five boroughs, and how to license a dog in NYC._

> LOW-COST VET, SPAY/NEUTER & NYC DOG LICENSING (contacts inline)

Free/low-cost veterinary care, spay-neuter, vaccine/microchip options, and the legally-required NYC dog license. Every dog 4+ months must be licensed; every dog owner must show proof of license + rabies in public. Verified against each provider's own site / NYC DOHMH / the ACC Low-Cost Vet Resources sheet on 2026-08-27. Confirm eligibility (many are income-qualified) and current pricing before you go.

chunks.heading: NYC DOG LICENSE - legally required (NYC Health Code 161.04)
chunks.text:
Mail to: NYC DOHMH Dog License, PO Box 22136, New York, NY 10087-2136. Check/money order payable to 'NYC DOHMH' (no cash).

Fees: $8.50/yr spayed-neutered (any age) OR dog under 4 months; $34.00/yr unaltered dog over 4 months; late fee $2.00/yr; replacement tag $1.00. May license up to 5 years at once.

Questions: call 311 (ask for the DOHMH Dog Licensing Unit). Leash law: max 6 ft in public; report issues via 311.

- How: apply/renew ONLINE at nyc.gov/doglicense (debit/credit/e-check), or mail a paper form (call 311 to have one mailed; forms in English + Spanish). You need proof of a current RABIES vaccine.
- In-person same-day licensing events (held across all 5 boroughs) waive the $2 late penalty and you won't be cited on-site - check the Same-Day Licensing/Vaccination schedule at nyc.gov/doglicense.

chunks.heading: CITYWIDE - free / low-cost SPAY-NEUTER
chunks.text:
- ASPCA Mobile Spay/Neuter + Community Clinics - free/low-cost s/n for dogs & cats across all 5 boroughs. Same-Day virtual WAITLIST (sign up 6:00 AM day-of at clinic.aspca.org/clinics/new-york-city). Phone (844) 692-7722. $0 with proof of public assistance; ~$125 without. Owner 18+, pet 2 months-9 yrs, no known medical issues. No walk-ins.
- The Toby Project - NYC's only org solely devoted to free/low-cost s/n; mobile vans + in-neighborhood clinics, works with DOHMH. Free s/n with proof of public assistance, reduced without; vaccines $8 (with s/n only). Email tobyprojectnyc@gmail.com (Bronx & Queens mobile scheduling) or (212) 315-5251; https://www.tobyproject.org/services.
- Humane Society of New York - full-service low-cost veterinary hospital + Animal Mukti FREE spay/neuter program + a free Pit Bull s/n program (100% covered). 306 East 59th St, NY 10022 (btwn 1st/2nd Ave). (212) 752-4842 / clinic (212) 752-4840, 9-5 by APPOINTMENT ONLY (allow 24-48 hrs for callback). info.HSNY@verizon.net; https://humanesocietyny.org.
- Friends of Animals - low-cost spay/neuter CERTIFICATES usable at participating NYC vets (you pay FoA, then use the certificate at a clinic; clinic may add charges for extras). (800) 321-7387; https://friendsofanimals.org/our-programs/spay-neuter.
- MAMA Coupon (Muffin's Pet Connection + Mayor's Alliance) - low-cost s/n coupon: ~$58 female / $45 male, includes s/n + rabies + eartip. Participating vets + guidelines at www.muffins.org/MAMA.htm.
- NYC DOHMH low-cost s/n index (authoritative list, updated periodically): https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/low-cost-spay-and-neuter-clinics.page.

chunks.heading: ASPCA COMMUNITY VETERINARY CLINICS - by borough (appointment only, income-qualified)
chunks.text:
(No dedicated ASPCA community clinic in Manhattan/Staten Island - use the mobile waitlist + citywide options above.)

- BRONX - ASPCA Community Veterinary Clinic, South Bronx: s/n + wellness by appointment for eligible dog/cat owners. Start via the Same-Day Waitlist at clinic.aspca.org/locations/new-york-city. (Low-cost urgent care at the ASPCA Animal Hospital requires household income \<= $50k.)
- BROOKLYN - ASPCA Community Veterinary Clinic (Lewyt), East New York: s/n + wellness by appointment for eligible owners. Same-Day Waitlist at clinic.aspca.org/locations/new-york-city.
- QUEENS - ASPCA Community Veterinary Clinic (Rachael Ray Foundation), Long Island City: s/n + wellness + routine care by appointment for eligible Queens residents. clinic.aspca.org/locations/new-york-city.

chunks.heading: BOROUGH low-cost VET CLINICS (from the ACC Low-Cost Vet Resources sheet, Jan 2025)
chunks.text:
- BROOKLYN - Animal Clinic of Bay Ridge: lower-cost vet care, 689 86th St, Brooklyn 11228, (718) 833-0700, animalclinicofbayridgebrooklyn.net.
- BROOKLYN - Sean Casey Animal Rescue runs low-cost vaccine/microchip clinics: 153 East 3rd St 11218, (718) 436-5163; nyanimalrescue.org.
- CITYWIDE - Banfield Pet Hospital: not free but lower-cost; e.g. Brooklyn 238 Atlantic Ave 11201; pricing at banfield.com. Free first vet visit for newly adopted pets.
- CITYWIDE - Petco Vetco / Vetco vaccine clinics: no exam fee; rabies ~$20, other vaccines ~$34; packages available. vetcoclinics.com.
- CITYWIDE - VIP Petcare clinics: no exam fee, single-vaccine or package pricing; find a location at vippetcare.com.
- WESTCHESTER-ADJACENT (nr Bronx) - Bully Baby Rescue runs free/low-cost s/n clinics (Port Chester): info@bullybabyrescue.org, (914) 565-1512.

chunks.heading: ACC COMMUNITY PETS PROGRAM - free help to keep pets with their families
chunks.text:
Free pop-up vaccine + microchip clinics in the Bronx and Queens: free rabies, DA2PP, and Bordetella (kennel cough) for dogs, free microchips, and referrals for free spay/neuter. Check the ACC events page for dates and locations.

Also offers: free dog training, tenant advocacy and pet-housing help, spay/neuter appointments, and connections to other agencies.

- ACC's Community Pets Program provides free resources to help owners care for their dogs. Contact via nycacc.org/programs/community-resources or ACC (212) 788-4000.

chunks.heading: LOW-COST DOG DENTAL (periodontal disease affects ~80% of dogs over age 3)
chunks.text:
Veterinary teaching hospitals + nonprofit clinics run ~$50-150 vs a ~$388 private-practice average - ask about pre-anesthetic bloodwork (required for dogs over 5 or with severe disease).

- Humane Society of NY - has a dedicated 'doggy dentist' doing dentals 4-5 days/week (~4 dogs/day); low-cost, volunteer-supported. Books up fast via a waitlist - call early. 306 E 59th St, (212) 752-4842.
- ASPCA Community Veterinary Clinics (S.Bronx 501 E 161st St / E.NY Brooklyn / LIC Queens) - subsidized dental cleanings + extractions alongside wellness, income \<=$50k. Waitlist via (844) 692-7722.
- BBAWC Rescue Clinic (Brooklyn Bridge Animal Welfare Coalition) - low-cost dentals + spay/neuter. bbawc.org/clinic, (917) 426-3335.

chunks.heading: PET FOOD / SUPPLIES (dog-specific pantries + directories)
chunks.text:
- ACC - may provide food, harnesses, and other supplies directly; ask Admissions (admissions@nycacc.org).
- ASPCA Community Engagement + Animal Haven Community Engagement Program - free/subsidized pet supplies incl. food for low-income New Yorkers (animalhaven.org, aspca.org).
- PAWS NY - operates a pet food pantry alongside its in-home care (pawsny.org, (212) 203-4760).
- Food Help NYC (nyc.gov/foodhelp) - find human food pantries; many also stock pet food. donateNYC Directory has a Pet Care/Food category.
- Pets of the Homeless (petsofthehomeless.org) - national org providing FREE pet food + vet/dental/emergency care specifically for pets of homeless + at-risk people; find NYC-area donation/host sites on their map.

chunks.heading: VACCINE + MICROCHIP EVENTS
chunks.text:
Petco Vetco / VIP Petcare (above) do walk-in vaccine + microchip clinics at many NYC pet stores - low cost, no exam fee.

- ACC hosts periodic low-cost vaccine + microchip + licensing events across the boroughs - check nycacc.org (events) and the DOHMH Same-Day Licensing/Vaccination schedule.
- Microchip registration is separate from implanting: after any chip event, register the chip with the microchip company (e.g. 24Petwatch 24pet.com free, HomeAgain homeagain.com) so your contact info is on file.

chunks.heading: VET-BILL FINANCIAL AID (when care is unaffordable)
chunks.text:
- NYSAVE (NY Save Animals in Veterinary Emergency) - NYC-SPECIFIC emergency funding for sick/injured pets of low-income NYC residents (all 5 boroughs). At/below NYC poverty level (about $41,100 for 1 person / $58,700 for a family of 4); you must first be denied by CareCredit/Scratchpay; ~$2,000/yr per household, paid to a participating vet. Apply: (917) 669-7281, info@nysave.org, nysave.org.
- AMC (Schwarzman Animal Medical Center, Manhattan) financial-assistance funds - Charlie's Patient Assistance Fund (free/subsidized EMERGENCY care), Buddy Fund (cancer), Cooper Fund (radiation), SAVE (seniors 65+), plus military/adopted-pet discounts. Pet must be seen at AMC; apply within 5 business days of treatment. funds@amcny.org, (212) 838-8100, amcny.org/financial-assistance.
- ASPCA Animal Hospital (AAH) - low-cost urgent care in NYC for owners with household income at or below $50,000 (bring EBT / SSI / VA / unemployment / TANF proof). Apply via aspca.org/nyc.
- RedRover Relief - grants (avg ~$250) toward urgent, life-threatening care; household income under $60,000/yr; paid to the vet. redrover.org/relief, (916) 429-2457.
- The Pet Fund - help for non-urgent care such as chronic conditions; contact BEFORE applying. info@thepetfund.com, (916) 443-6007, thepetfund.com.
- Frankie's Friends - grants for lifesaving emergency or specialty care (pet already seen by a vet, good prognosis). frankiesfriends.org/apply-for-assistance-3.
- Waggle - vet-bill crowdfunding; 100% of funds go to the vet. waggle.org.
- The Humane Society of NY - some cases receive full or partial funding through its Animal Emergency Appeal; ask when booking. 306 East 59th St, NY 10022, (212) 752-4842.
- Brown Dog Foundation (browndogfoundation.org), The Mosby Foundation (themosbyfoundation.org), Onyx & Breezy

chunks.heading: PET INSURANCE (for planning ahead, not an unpaid bill you already have)
chunks.text:
Pet insurance reimburses a percentage of future covered vet costs after you pay the vet; it does NOT cover pre-existing conditions, so it helps most when started while a dog is young and healthy. Compare deductible, reimbursement %, annual limit, and what's excluded.

Others widely reviewed for 2026: Embrace, Figo, Lemonade, Spot, Pumpkin, Fetch, MetLife. Get 2-3 quotes and read each policy's exclusions before choosing.

Tip: ask the insurer in writing how they define a pre-existing condition, and whether curable conditions (e.g. an ear infection) can be covered later.

Most subsidized spay/neuter and clinic programs are income-qualified and/or waitlist-based, and capacity is limited. Confirm eligibility, what's included, and current price when you book - certificate programs sometimes add charges for vaccines, older-pet bloodwork, pregnancy, or take-home medications.

- Trupanion - trupanion.com, (855) 591-3100. Per-condition deductible; can pay the vet directly at participating clinics; 90% reimbursement.
- Healthy Paws - healthypaws.com, (855) 898-8991. Annual deductible, unlimited annual coverage, 70-90% reimbursement; fast claims.
- ASPCA Pet Health Insurance - aspcapetinsurance.com, (866) 204-6764. Customizable; optional wellness add-on; up to 270 days to submit a claim.
- Nationwide - petinsurance.com, (877) 738-7874. Long-standing; some plans cover lost-pet advertising; military discount.
- Pets Best - petsbest.com, (877) 738-7237. Direct-vet-pay option; military discount.

guides.title: Dog behaviour, training and legal questions
guides.summary: Behaviour help, bite reporting, breed rules and housing law.

chunks.heading: Dog behaviour, training and legal questions
chunks.text:
_Behaviour help, bite reporting, breed rules and housing law._

> TRAINING, BEHAVIOR & LEGAL RESOURCES (contacts inline)

Training, behavior support, service/therapy-dog programs, and NYC legal/reporting resources for dog owners. Verified against each provider's own site, ACC, DOHMH, and NY State law on 2026-08-27. Confirm current details before relying. This is general information, not legal advice.

chunks.heading: FREE / LOW-COST BEHAVIOR + TRAINING
chunks.text:
- ACC Community Pets Program - free dog training (in-person or Zoom/FaceTime) via partner trainers, plus free behavior guides at nycacc.org/services/behavior-resources. Contact: admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000.
- Bideawee + GoodPup - subsidized virtual 1-on-1 positive-reinforcement training; first week free at links.goodpup.com/shelter/Bideawee10; 24/7 trainer chat. Bideawee: bideawee.org, (866) 262-8133.
- ASPCA behavior guides - free articles on common dog behaviors at aspca.org/pet-care/dog-care, plus the ASPCA Virtual Pet Behaviorist archive.
- Muddy Paws Rescue behavior resources ('Pack Perks') - open to the public at muddypawsrescue.org.

chunks.heading: HOW TO CHOOSE A POSITIVE-REINFORCEMENT TRAINER
chunks.text:
Helpful credentials: CPDT-KA / CPDT-KSA (Cert. Council for Professional Dog Trainers), KPA-CTP (Karen Pryor Academy), CBCC-KA, or a Veterinary Behaviorist (DACVB) for complex cases.

Many owners look for reward-based, force-free methods and ask a trainer about their approach to reactivity, counter-conditioning, and desensitization before booking.

- Directories: ccpdt.org, apdt.com (Assoc. of Professional Dog Trainers), iaabc.org (Intl. Assoc. of Animal Behavior Consultants), dacvb.org (board-certified veterinary behaviorists).

chunks.heading: NYC BEHAVIOR + REACTIVITY SPECIALISTS
chunks.text:
- Wag the Dog NYC - reward-based; group reactive-dog class + private work on reactivity, separation anxiety, and fearful dogs. wagthedognyc.com.
- Instinct Dog Behavior & Training - behavior-focused (leash reactivity, fear); Manhattan + Brooklyn. instinctdogtraining.com.
- School for the Dogs - force-free training, Manhattan. schoolforthedogs.com.
- Empire of the Dog - training + behavior, Brooklyn. empireofthedog.com.
- Veterinary behaviorists (for complex cases + medication): find one at dacvb.org.

chunks.heading: FREE SERVICE DOGS - veterans / people with disabilities (NY-serving)
chunks.text:
These organizations provide dogs at no cost to the recipient; the ADA does not require any certificate or registration for a service dog.

- America's VetDogs - Smithtown, NY: free service + guide dogs for veterans, active-duty, and first responders (PTSD, mobility, hearing/vision, seizures); all costs including transport covered. vetdogs.org, (631) 930-9000.
- Guide Dog Foundation - Smithtown, NY: free guide dogs for people who are blind or low-vision. guidedog.org, (631) 930-9000.
- Canine Companions - Northeast Region (Medford, NY): free service dogs for adults, children, and veterans with disabilities. canine.org, (631) 561-0200.
- Putnam Service Dogs - Carmel, NY: free service dogs (mobility + veteran support) for people in the NY area. putnamservicedogs.org.
- Pups4Patriots (American Humane) - free service dogs for veterans. americanhumane.org, (866) 242-1877.
- PAVE (Paws Assisting Veterans) - free service dogs for veterans. paveusa.org.

chunks.heading: THERAPY + EMOTIONAL-SUPPORT DOGS
chunks.text:
Emotional Support Animal (ESA): housing protections may apply with a letter from a licensed provider; an ESA is different from a service dog and does not have public-access rights.

- Therapy-dog certification (to volunteer with your own dog at hospitals/schools): The Good Dog Foundation (NYC-based, thegooddogfoundation.org), Pet Partners (petpartners.org), Alliance of Therapy Dogs (therapydogs.com).

chunks.heading: QUALITY-OF-LIFE + GRIEF SUPPORT
chunks.text:
- Quality-of-life assessment tools and end-of-life guidance: talk with your veterinarian, or a veterinary behaviorist at dacvb.org for behavior-related questions.
- Pet-loss grief support: ASPCA Pet Loss resources (aspca.org), Cornell Pet Loss Support Hotline (508-839-7966), Lap of Love pet-loss support (lapoflove.com/pet-loss-support).

chunks.heading: NYC BITE REPORTING (Health Code 11.03)
chunks.text:
In NYC, animal bites are reported to the Health Department within 24 hours - by anyone involved.

After a bite, a dog is typically observed for 10 days for rabies. Anyone bitten should seek medical advice, especially if the dog's rabies vaccination can't be confirmed.

- How to report: call 311, or the DOHMH Animal Bite Unit at (646) 364-1799 (or DOHMH (212) 676-2483), or file online at the NYC Health Department animal-bite reporting page. Keep the confirmation number.

chunks.heading: NY STATE LAW - what owners may want to know (Ag & Markets Law 108 & 123)
chunks.text:
New York State (not a NYC breed rule) sets the process for how a dog may be legally classified after a serious incident; a complaint goes to a dog-control or police officer and a judge decides after a hearing.

There can be civil penalties for the owner after a bite, and higher penalties if serious injury results. Details and amounts change over time - confirm current law with an attorney or the DOHMH.

NYC has no breed ban. NYCHA and some landlords/insurers set their own breed or weight limits, which is a housing/contract matter rather than a city law.

chunks.heading: LEGAL AID + REFERRALS
chunks.text:
To report suspected animal cruelty in NYC: call 911 or 311.

- Animal Legal Defense Fund - resource lists + referrals: aldf.org.
- ASPCA - has at times provided legal help in NYC cases; ask for a current referral at aspca.org or (212) 876-7700.
- Housing / breed-restriction disputes: ACC assists with tenant/landlord and NYCHA matters (admissions@nycacc.org, (212) 788-4000); tenant legal help via 311 or NYC Housing Court Answers, housingcourtanswers.org, (212) 962-4795.

chunks.heading: BREED / HOUSING-RESTRICTION SUPPORT
chunks.text:
A dog-DNA test (Embark, Wisdom Panel) is sometimes used to document a mixed-breed dog's makeup for a landlord or insurer; results are not guaranteed to satisfy any given policy.

- Pet-inclusive + pet-friendly housing search: petsandhousing.org (Pet-Inclusive Housing Initiative).

chunks.heading: ACC tenant advocacy (above) can help work through a housing issue before other steps.
chunks.text: Legal information here is general and changes over time - confirm current rules with a NY attorney or the DOHMH. This is not legal advice.

guides.title: Lost or found a dog
guides.summary: The first hours matter most. Where to look, who to call, and how microchips help.

chunks.heading: Lost or found a dog
chunks.text:
_The first hours matter most. Where to look, who to call, and how microchips help._

> LOST & FOUND DOGS + MICROCHIP REGISTRIES (contacts inline)

Act FAST - most reunions happen when owners move quickly. A microchip only works if it's REGISTERED and current. Verified against ACC, Mayor's Alliance, Petco Love Lost, and 24Petwatch on 2026-08-27.

chunks.heading: LOST A DOG - do all of these NOW
chunks.text:
4. Post flyers (photo + your phone) around the neighborhood, vet offices, pet stores; post to local Facebook lost-pet groups + Nextdoor; list on PawBoost, FidoAlert, Pet FBI (free).

5. Do NOT chase a scared dog - it makes them bolt. Sit low, look away, toss high-value food; for dogs, leaving out your worn (stinky) clothing + grilling smelly meat can draw them back. Leave a light on and someone home.

- 1. Check ACC 24/7: search + file a LOST report at nycacc.org/services/lost-and-found - ACC takes in found pets citywide; your dog could already be there. Also call ACC (212) 788-4000.
- 2. Report + search on Petco Love Lost (FREE, uses facial recognition): petcolove.org/lost - upload a clear FACE photo; it auto-matches against found reports from shelters + neighbors and generates printable flyers.
- 3. Update your MICROCHIP: call your chip company, confirm your contact info is current, and mark the pet LOST. Don't know the company? Use the AAHA Microchip Registry Lookup (aaha.org/petmicrochiplookup) with the chip number.

chunks.heading: FOUND A DOG
chunks.text:
Secure the dog safely if you can. Check for ID tags + a dog-license tag.

Get it SCANNED for a microchip - any vet office or ACC shelter will scan free; if chipped, the chip company locates the owner.

After business hours, or if the dog is sick/injured/dangerous: call 911 and a dispatcher will assist.

You can bring a found dog to any ACC Care Center during business hours (call ahead). Check lost-pet apps/Facebook groups to match it to an owner searching.

- Report as FOUND on Petco Love Lost (petcolove.org/lost) and file a FOUND report on ACC (nycacc.org/services/lost-and-found). Call ACC before bringing a found pet in: (212) 788-4000.

chunks.heading: MICROCHIP REGISTRIES - register the chip (implanting is not registering)
chunks.text:
KEY: a chip must be updated MANUALLY every time you move or change phone/email. An unregistered or outdated chip cannot reunite you with your dog.

- 24Petwatch (by PetPlace) - North America's largest registry; FREE registration, no mandatory fees. Register/update/report lost at petplace.com/pet-microchip-registry or 24pet.com. Recovery specialists run real-time found searches.
- HomeAgain - homeagain.com; enrolled chips also WAIVE the ASPCA Poison Control consultation fee.
- AKC Reunite - akcreunite.org, (800) 252-7894; lifetime registration.
- Petkey / Save This Life / Michelson Found Animals (foundanimals.org - free) - other registries.
- AAHA Universal Lookup - petmicrochiplookup.org: enter a chip number to find which registry it's in (doesn't store owner data, points you to the right company).

chunks.heading: NYC STRAY-HOLD + PREVENTION
chunks.text:
NY stray-hold: found pets are generally reported to animal control (ACC) and held a minimum number of days before becoming adoptable - confirm current hold period with ACC.

NOTE: Petco Love Lost is free and the single highest-leverage step (facial-recognition matching across NYC shelters + community) - do it first alongside the ACC report.

- Prevention: license your dog (nyc.gov/doglicense), keep a physical ID tag on the collar, register and maintain the microchip, use a well-fitted martingale collar or harness, and keep a recent full-body photo on your phone.

chunks.heading: Breed-specific dog rescue
chunks.text:
_Rescues that focus on a particular breed or group of breeds._

> BREED-SPECIFIC DOG RESCUES serving NYC (contacts inline)

Use when an adopter or surrenderer wants (or has) a specific breed/type. Most are breed-club networks that cover NYC through a regional/NYC-area volunteer coordinator rather than a local shelter, so ALWAYS confirm current NYC-area capacity and intake. All are ACC New Hope partners unless noted. Verified against each org's own site / the ACC New Hope list on 2026-08-27.

"BULLY" / MOLOSSER BREEDS - what this group includes (read first)

'Bully breeds' refers to a family of breeds (the molossers/mastiff-type dogs), not only pit bulls. It includes: American Pit Bull Terrier, American Staffordshire Terrier, Staffordshire Bull Terrier, American Bully, American Bulldog, English/Olde English Bulldog, French Bulldog, Boston Terrier, Bull Terrier, Boxer, Rottweiler, Cane Corso, Dogo Argentino, Presa Canario, Bullmastiff/Mastiff, Dogue de Bordeaux, Great Dane, and their mixes.

The label describes body type, not temperament - individual dogs vary widely, and behavior is shaped far more by training, handling, and environment than by breed. The rescues below welcome the full range.

This tab lists all-'bully' rescues first (they take the whole group), then breed-specific groups within it (Rottweiler, Boxer, Cane Corso, Mastiff/Great Dane, Bulldog, Doberman, Bull Terrier).

guides.title: Found injured or orphaned wildlife

chunks.heading: Found injured or orphaned wildlife
chunks.text:
_Only licensed rehabilitators may legally handle wild animals. Where to take them, and what not to do._

> Wildlife rehabilitation - critical and legally distinct

The rule first: only NYS-licensed wildlife rehabilitators may legally handle wild animals in New York, and most wild animals cannot legally be kept as pets. Wildlife is a rehabilitation-and-release matter, NOT an adoption matter. If you find injured, sick or orphaned wildlife, contact a licensed rehabber for advice before handling it - some species need special handling and some carry diseases transmissible to people.

NYC's main wildlife hospital - The Wild Bird Fund

565 Columbus Avenue (between 87th & 88th), New York, NY 10024. Phone 646-306-2862. Open daily 9am-7pm. NYC's only wildlife rehabilitation & education center. Takes injured/sick/orphaned wild birds AND small mammals (pigeons, waterfowl, raptors, songbirds, squirrels, opossums) 7 days a week; walk-in, no appointment needed (leave a message if arriving near closing). Found-a-bird guidance: wildbirdfund.org/how-to-help/rescue. IG @wildbirdfund.

LIMITATION: WBF CANNOT take exotic birds (budgerigars, parrots) or domestic birds (chickens, quail, domestic geese, tame doves). It CAN take rock/domestic pigeons. For exotic or domestic birds WBF can't take, Animal Care Centers of NYC (311 / 212-788-4000) is the drop-off (as of 2022): chukars, chickens, domestic geese, budgerigars, etc.

chunks.heading: NYC-area licensed rehabbers - raptors & general (state + federally licensed):
chunks.text:
Can't transport an injured bird yourself?

- Urban Park Rangers - will try to pick up a bird in a NYC park (priority to less-common birds; limited resources for raptors outside parks). Primary 646-613-1200; Manhattan 212-628-2345 (9am-5pm daily); nycgovparks.org.
- Email the Urban Wildlife Alliance helpline: helpline@urbanwildlifenyc.org (urbanwildlifenyc.org). NYC Bird Alliance also maintains an authoritative NYC injured-bird routing page (all listed rehabbers accept birds; many take other wildlife): https://nycbirdalliance.org/take-action/help-a-bird-in-trouble/nyc-region-animal-hospitals-and-rehabilitation-centers.

chunks.heading: NYC veterinarians who will see WILDLIFE by appointment (rare - most vets won't):
chunks.text:
The official directory - NYS DEC 'Find a Wildlife Rehabilitator'

Rabies Vector Species - raccoons, skunks, bats (important NYC limitation)

There are NO NYC-licensed wildlife rehabilitators who can take raccoons, skunks or bats, because these are classified as Rabies Vector Species (RVS) in New York and require a special RVS license. Licensed RVS rehabbers exist in surrounding counties - find them via the DEC rehabber search (select 'bats, raccoons, or skunks' and search county by county). For an RVS animal in the city: stay away, do not touch or feed it, call 311 and ask for the Urban Park Rangers, and file the parks online report; call 911 too if there's a risk to people or the animal. If you've had contact with an RVS animal, contact your doctor immediately. Any mammal can carry rabies. (For coyote questions: Gotham Coyote Project - seeing a coyote in NYC is usually not cause for alarm.)

Second directory - NYS Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (NYSWRC)

Marine mammals & sea turtles (seals, whales, dolphins, porpoises, sea turtles)

Wild turtles specifically

What to do / what NOT to do with an injured wild animal

DO: note the exact location; if safe, contain a small bird/mammal in a ventilated box in a warm, dark, quiet place; keep it away from pets and children; call a licensed rehabber or the Wild Bird Fund promptly. Do NOT offer food or water unless a rehabber tells you to.

DON'T: try to raise or keep wildlife yourself (illegal and usually fatal for the animal); handle bats, raccoons or other rabies-vector species with bare hands (call DEC/animal control); or assume a lone fawn or fledgling is orphaned - many are not, so check with a rehabber first.

- Vinegar Hill Veterinary Group (DUMBO/Brooklyn Heights) - Drs. Sara Neumann & Amy Adelman see wildlife by appoin

guides.title: Exotic pet emergencies
guides.summary: Rabbits, birds, reptiles and small mammals need an exotic-capable vet. Call ahead.

chunks.heading: Exotic pet emergencies
chunks.text:
_Rabbits, birds, reptiles and small mammals need an exotic-capable vet. Call ahead._

> Exotic-vet & emergency care

Why a separate list: most general small-animal vets do NOT treat rabbits, birds, reptiles or other exotics. Exotic species hide illness and decline fast, so line up a rabbit/bird/'exotics-savvy' vet BEFORE you need one. Confirm each clinic still sees your species, and their current hours and emergency policy, by phone on the clinic's own line before relying on it.

chunks.heading: Finding an exotics vet you can trust
chunks.text:
- Rabbit Rescue & Rehab keeps a rabbit-savvy vet-care page: rabbitrescueandrehab.org/vet-care.
- Bunnies & Beyond keeps a NYC rabbit/guinea-pig vet list: bunniesandbeyond.org/vets.
- NYTTS keeps a turtle/reptile Care & Veterinarians page: nytts.org (Care/Veterinarians).
- The Association of Avian Veterinarians (aav.org) and the Association of Reptilian & Amphibian Veterinarians (arav.org) both have 'find a vet' tools for board-experienced exotic vets.

chunks.heading: 24/7 emergency + specialty (call ahead - confirm they take your species that night):
chunks.text: - The Schwarzman Animal Medical Center (AMC), 510 East 62nd Street, Manhattan, NY 10065 - (212) 838-8100 - 24/7/365 ER with a dedicated Avian & Exotic Pet Medicine Service treating birds, reptiles, guinea pigs, rabbits and other small mammals (amcny.org/pet-owners/specialties/avian-exotic-pet-medicine). No appointment needed for emergency/urgent care; a new ER opened Dec 2025. One of the few NYC ERs with in-house, board-certified exotics specialists and CT/MRI/ultrasound/endoscopy on site. Also accepts injured raptors and waterfowl (per NYC Bird Alliance). AMC's exotic service (est. 1984) was NYC's first; treats birds, rabbits, guinea pigs, ferrets, small rodents and reptiles.

chunks.heading: Dedicated exotics day-practice (routine + sick visits, not 24/7):
chunks.text:
- The Center for Avian & Exotic Medicine, 562 Columbus Avenue, Manhattan, NY 10024 - (212) 501-8750 - open 7 days 9am-7pm. NYC's only exclusively avian & exotic veterinary hospital (a calm, dog/cat-free environment). Treats birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, small mammals, small ruminants, and wildlife-as-pets (e.g. squirrels, pigeons); offers TeleVet for established patients. The natural complement to AMC's ER for non-emergency exotic care. (On Columbus Ave, near the Wild Bird Fund.)
- Long Island Bird & Exotics Vet Clinic (Nassau County) - the only avian & exotic hospital in Nassau; serves all of NYC (Manhattan, Queens, Brooklyn, Bronx, Staten Island) plus Westchester/NJ/CT. Treats birds, reptiles, parrots, sugar gliders, rabbits, chinchillas and other small mammals; offers endoscopy, anesthesia, minimally invasive surgery, emergency services, MEDICAL BOARDING and grooming (birdexoticsvet.com). A strong exotics-only option for outer-borough/LI residents.
- Vinegar Hill Veterinary Group, 57 Front St, Unit 101, Brooklyn (DUMBO) 11201 - (718) 797-6875 - Mon-Fri 8am-8pm, Sat-Sun 10am-5pm (2nd location in Brooklyn Heights); vhvetgroup.com. A full-service clinic with the equipment and expertise to treat exotic & avian species (incubators, oxygen therapy, nebulization) alongside cats/dogs; sees guinea pigs, turtles, hedgehogs and birds, and treats some WILDLIFE by appointment (Drs. Neumann & Adelman). The most convenient exotics-capable full-service option in Brooklyn.
- BluePearl and other regional emergency hospitals list exotic capability unevenly - always phone first to confirm an exotics-capable clinician is on that shift.

chunks.heading: Poison control (exotics are highly sensitive - lilies, avocado, teflon fumes, many houseplants can be fatal):
chunks.text:
These lines cover exotic pets, not just cats and dogs. Have the species, weight, and the substance/amount ready.

Note on wildlife

- ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: (888) 426-4435 - 24/7 (a consultation fee may apply). aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control.
- Pet Poison Helpline: (855) 764-7661 - 24/7 (fee applies).
- A wild animal is not a candidate for a pet-clinic visit - route it to a licensed wildlife rehabber or the Wild Bird Fund (646-306-2862). See the Wildlife rehabilitation tab.

guides.title: What you can legally keep in New York City
guides.summary: Which animals are legal as pets in NYC, and which must go to a rehabber or sanctuary.

chunks.heading: What you can legally keep in New York City
chunks.text:
_Which animals are legal as pets in NYC, and which must go to a rehabber or sanctuary._

> Species care & legality (NYC / NYS)

This tab is orientation, not legal advice. NYC and NYS rules change; confirm current status with NYC Health, NYC ACC, or NYS DEC before acquiring or rehoming an animal. General picture as of the last-verified date:

chunks.heading: Prohibited as pets in NYC (illegal to keep - a non-exhaustive list):
chunks.text:
- NYC Health Code bans keeping most wild and exotic animals as pets. Ferrets specifically are banned in NEW YORK CITY under the NYC Health Code (Article 161.01, which lists ferrets among prohibited animals), even though ferrets are legal in the rest of NEW YORK STATE including Long Island. The NYC Board of Health considered lifting the ban in 2015 and voted to keep it; it remained in place as of the last-verified date (confirm current status with NYC Health before acquiring or rehoming a ferret in the five boroughs). Other weasel-family animals - minks, skunks, badgers, wolverines, mongooses - are likewise barred in NYC.
- Also prohibited as pets in NYC: most non-human primates, many reptiles (venomous snakes, large constrictors, crocodilians/alligators), and most wild carnivores.
- Roosters are generally not permitted in NYC residential settings; farm animals (pigs, goats, sheep, cows, including 'teacup'/'mini' pigs) are barred from most residential zoning.
- Venomous reptiles and dangerous wild animals are prohibited.

chunks.heading: Native NY wildlife & native reptiles/amphibians:
chunks.text:
- Most native wildlife cannot legally be kept. Injured/orphaned wildlife must go to a NYS-licensed wildlife rehabilitator (see the Wildlife rehabilitation tab).
- NYS DEC now requires a permit to keep ANY reptile or amphibian native to New York, including all 12 native NY turtle species. It is illegal to sell native NY reptiles/amphibians - report violations to DEC at 1-800-847-7332.

chunks.heading: Generally legal companion exotics (with care caveats):
chunks.text:
- Rabbits, guinea pigs, rats, mice, hamsters, gerbils, chinchillas: legal in NYC; all need species-specific housing/diet and exotics-savvy vet care. Rabbits and guinea pigs live 8-12+ years. (Note: unlike those, ferrets are NOT legal in NYC - see the prohibited list above.)
- Companion birds (parrots, budgies, cockatiels, finches, doves): legal; parrots can outlive their owners and go through multiple homes - a lifetime commitment.
- Many non-native reptiles kept as pets (bearded dragons, corn snakes, ball pythons, leopard geckos) are legal, but red-eared sliders create a serious surrender/dumping problem and must never be released.

chunks.heading: Authoritative care & rule sources:
chunks.text:
- House Rabbit Society: rabbit.org (diet, housing, health). NYC chapter: rabbitrescueandrehab.org.
- NYTTS turtle/tortoise care & the DEC native-reptile regulations overview at nytts.org.
- NYS DEC wildlife & licensed-rehabilitator info: dec.ny.gov.
- NYC ACC (surrender, adoption, guinea pigs/small animals): nycacc.org.
- Confirm NYC-specific pet legality with NYC Health (nyc.gov/health).

guides.title: Help paying for veterinary care
guides.summary: Grants, funds and low-cost options when you cannot afford treatment.

chunks.heading: Help paying for veterinary care
chunks.text:
_Grants, funds and low-cost options when you cannot afford treatment._

> Financial aid, low-cost care, insurance & food help (exotic-specific)

Why this tab: exotic vet care costs 2-3x standard pet care, far fewer clinics treat exotics, and most aid programs are written for cats and dogs. Below are the programs that actually cover exotics (birds, rabbits, small mammals, reptiles), plus the general funds that don't exclude them. Apply to SEVERAL at once - funds are limited and run out. Grants are paid to the veterinarian, not to you. Confirm eligibility and current status before relying on any single one.

chunks.heading: EXOTIC-SPECIFIC vet-bill funds (rare - these actually name exotics):
chunks.text:
- AMC (Schwarzman Animal Medical Center) - Honey Bunny and Rou Fund: subsidized SPECIALTY care specifically for RABBITS (and German Shepherds) of owners with limited means. One pet per household per 12 months. Pet must first be seen by an AMC vet; apply within 5 business days of starting treatment; tri-state residency (NY/NJ/CT); no outstanding AMC balance; can't hold another AMC grant. funds@amcny.org, (212) 838-8100, amcny.org/financial-assistance.
- AMC - Kiki White Umbrella Cockatoo Avian Fund: subsidizes specialty care for ALL BIRDS of families with limited means. Same rules as above (AMC exam first, 5-business-day deadline, tri-state, one pet per household per 12 months). This is one of the very few bird-specific vet funds anywhere. funds@amcny.org.
- AMC - Charlie's Patient Assistance Fund (emergency care, any species), the Buddy Fund (cancer, any species), the Monty and Minny Fund (rehabilitation), and SAVE (owners 65+): all open to exotic pets under the same eligibility rules. Start with AMC's Eligibility Application at amcny.org/financial-assistance (income threshold about $50k/household).

chunks.heading: GENERAL vet-bill funds that cover exotics (birds, rabbits, guinea pigs, etc.):
chunks.text:
- RedRover Relief - urgent/life-threatening care grants (avg ~$250); explicitly assists birds, rabbits and guinea pigs, not just cats/dogs; household income under ~$60k; paid to the vet. redrover.org/relief, (916) 429-2457. Also has a domestic-violence/pets program.
- The Pet Fund - non-urgent / chronic conditions for domestic animals (contact BEFORE treatment). info@thepetfund.com, (916) 443-6007, thepetfund.com.
- Frankie's Friends - lifesaving emergency or specialty care; pet already seen by a vet with a good prognosis. frankiesfriends.org/apply-for-assistance.
- The Mosby Foundation, Brown Dog Foundation, Onyx & Breezy Foundation - additional illness/injury funds that consider companion animals broadly; read each fund's species scope before applying.
- Waggle - vet-bill crowdfunding, 100% to the vet (waggle.org). Dial 211 or nyc.gov/211 for a live operator with current local assistance programs.

chunks.heading: For RESCUES (not individuals):
chunks.text: - AMC to the Rescue - subsidized specialty care for animals in the care of rescue groups whose health blocks adoption (amcny.org/amc-to-the-rescue). AMC also gives a 20% specialty-services discount to any 501(c)(3) animal nonprofit that presents an authorization letter on its letterhead + its IRS determination letter.

chunks.heading: Payment plans (accepted at most NYC vets, incl. exotics practices):
chunks.text: - CareCredit - healthcare credit card; carecredit.com or (800) 677-0718. Scratchpay - simple plans, soft credit check; scratchpay.com. Many aid funds require you to try/deny CareCredit or Scratchpay first.

chunks.heading: LOW-COST exotic care (few and far between - most low-cost clinics do NOT see exotics):
chunks.text:
- Sean Casey Animal Rescue (153 East 3rd St, Brooklyn 11218; (718) 436-5163) runs low-cost vaccine/microchip clinics and takes in exotics; ask what species/services are covered.
- The Center for Avian & Exotic Medicine (562 Columbus Ave; (212) 501-8750) - not free, but the dedicated exotics day-practice; ask about payment plans + wellness packages to spread cost.
- Rabbit and bird rescues in the main directory (Rabbit Rescue & Rehab, All About Rabbits Rescue, Bunnies & Beyond, Northeast Avian Rescue) keep vetted rabbit/avian-savvy vet lists and can point to the most affordable exotic vets.
- ACC (nycacc.org / 311) provides some low-cost services and takes in small animals; its Community Pets program offers keep-your-pet support - ask whether it extends to your species.

chunks.heading: EXOTIC PET INSURANCE (plan ahead - does NOT cover pre-existing conditions, so start while the animal is young/healthy):
chunks.text:
- Nationwide (petinsurance.com, (877) 738-7874) - the main insurer that covers birds, reptiles and many small mammals; the largest participating exotic-vet network. Ask specifically for its Avian & Exotic plan.
- Pet Assure (petassure.com) - not insurance but a veterinary DISCOUNT plan (usually 25% off in-house services) that covers virtually ANY species incl. exotics, with no pre-existing-condition exclusion; only works at participating vets - confirm your exotic vet accepts it.
- Some mainstream insurers (ASPCA Pet Health Insurance, others) cover certain small mammals/rabbits but not all exotics - always confirm species eligibility in writing before enrolling. Exotic wellness add-ons can cover beak/nail trims and routine exotic exams.
- Ask any insurer, in writing: which species you cover, how you define a pre-existing condition, and whether a curable condition can be covered later. Get 2-3 quotes and read the exclusions.

chunks.heading: FOOD & SUPPLY help (species-appropriate):
chunks.text:
How to use aid effectively: get a written itemized estimate + proof of need (SNAP/Medicaid/income), then apply to MULTIPLE programs the same day. For an AMC fund, the pet must be seen at AMC and you must apply within 5 business days of starting treatment - so raise it with AMC staff immediately, not after the fact.

- Rescue Chewy wishlists / supply drives (e.g. Bunnies & Beyond) and rescue care pages provide correct-diet guidance - rabbits need unlimited grass hay, guinea pigs need vitamin C + a companion, many 'pet-store' foods are harmful.
- ACC food pantry (Bronx Resource Center) + the ASPCA / Food Bank For NYC partnership (250+ pantries citywide via foodbanknyc.org) distribute pet food - ask whether they stock rabbit/small-animal/bird food specifically.
- Feeding Pets of the Homeless (petsofthehomeless.org) and PAWS NY (pawsny.org, (212) 203-4760) help people in crisis or with mobility limits keep and feed their animals; ask about exotics.

guides.title: Rehoming a rabbit, bird, reptile or small animal
guides.summary: Never release a domestic animal outdoors. Where to surrender responsibly.

chunks.heading: Rehoming a rabbit, bird, reptile or small animal
chunks.text:
_Never release a domestic animal outdoors. Where to surrender responsibly._

> Owner support & surrender prevention (exotic-specific)

The single most important message: NEVER release a domestic animal to the wild. Domestic rabbits, king/white pigeons, red-eared sliders, goldfish and farmed birds released outdoors almost always die (predators, cars, starvation, cold) and can spread disease or disrupt native ecosystems. There is always a better path than release, dumping, or handing an animal to a pet store 'feeder' pipeline.

chunks.heading: Why these surrenders happen - and the humane framing:
chunks.text:
- 'Easter bunny' rabbits: bought as impulse/holiday gifts, then surrendered when the ~10-year commitment, indoor housing, rabbit-savvy vet care and spay/neuter needs become clear. Rabbits are fragile, dislike being picked up, and are seldom suitable as children's 'starter pets.'
- Red-eared slider turtles: sold tiny and cheap, they grow large, live decades, and are invasive/illegal to release. Rescues are overwhelmed with them; rehoming can take a long time.
- 'Teacup'/'mini' pigs: marketed as staying small; they grow into large animals that are illegal to keep in most NYC residential zoning and need farmed-animal sanctuary placement.
- Roosters & backyard poultry: chicks bought at markets/feed stores turn out to be roosters (illegal/impractical in most NYC housing) and need sanctuary, not release.

chunks.heading: Keep-the-animal help (surrender prevention):
chunks.text:
- Rabbit Rescue & Rehab offers surrender-prevention coaching, care techniques and adopter-screening help (nyc.metro.rabbits@gmail.com) - most owners who felt they had to give up a bun find care can be made far easier.
- Reenie's Rabbit Rescue offers bonding, boarding, grooming and advice (845-591-7751).
- Bunnies & Beyond, All About Rabbits Rescue, NYTTS and Empty Cages Collective all provide species-appropriate care education (housing, diet, bonding) aimed at keeping animals in their homes.

chunks.heading: Safe surrender paths (never release-to-wild):
chunks.text:
Species-appropriate food & supply help

Chewy wishlists and rescue supply drives (e.g. Bunnies & Beyond's Chewy wishlist) and rescue care pages provide correct diet guidance - e.g. rabbits need unlimited grass hay (not a pellet-heavy diet), guinea pigs need vitamin C and a bonded companion, and many 'pet-store' foods are actively harmful. Ask the relevant rescue's care page before changing a diet.

- Rabbits/guinea pigs: Rabbit Rescue & Rehab, All About Rabbits Rescue, Bunnies & Beyond, Empty Cages Collective, or Animal Care Centers of NYC (nycacc.org). Screen adopters carefully if rehoming yourself (protect against 'feeder'/bait uses).
- Turtles/reptiles: NY Turtle & Tortoise Society (qanda@nytts.org), Earthlings NYC Turtle Team, or Stray Pride.
- Birds: Northeast Avian Rescue, Long Island Parrot Society placement program; feral/domestic pigeons -\> NYCPRC.
- Farmed animals/poultry/pigs: Woodstock Farm Sanctuary (AnimalHelp@woodstocksanctuary.org) or Catskill Animal Sanctuary (confirm capacity first).
- Any species you can't place: Animal Care Centers of NYC is the open-admission safety net (nycacc.org / 311).

guides.title: Lost or found a rabbit, bird or reptile
guides.summary: Where to report, and how to tell a lost pet from a wild animal.

chunks.heading: Lost or found a rabbit, bird or reptile
chunks.text:
_Where to report, and how to tell a lost pet from a wild animal._

> Lost-found & microchip / ID

Exotics can be microchipped and can be lost or found just like cats and dogs - but the search channels differ by species. Act fast: small animals and birds are vulnerable outdoors.

chunks.heading: Birds (parrots, companion birds):
chunks.text:
- Microchipping: larger parrots can be microchipped by an avian vet; leg bands also carry ID. Register the chip and note the band number.
- Lost/found parrots: Long Island Parrot Society runs a Lost & Found and placement program (liparrots.org). Post to regional parrot groups and to 911 Parrot Alert (911parrotalert.com), a national lost-and-found bird network.
- A found domestic bird outdoors needs shelter fast - contain it safely and contact an avian vet or rescue.

chunks.heading: Pigeons & doves (feral vs domestic):
chunks.text: - A tame, all-white or oddly-colored pigeon that lets you approach is almost certainly a domestic/king pigeon that cannot survive in the wild - it needs rescue. Contact NYC Pigeon Rescue Central (nycprc.org Help Request form + Google Group) or bring it to the Wild Bird Fund. Banded racing/homing pigeons carry a band that can trace an owner.

chunks.heading: Rabbits & small mammals:
chunks.text: - Rabbits can be microchipped by a rabbit-savvy vet; register the chip. A found domestic rabbit outdoors is a rescue situation (they cannot survive as strays) - contact Rabbit Rescue & Rehab, All About Rabbits Rescue or Bunnies & Beyond, or ACC. Contain it safely and out of the heat/cold.

chunks.heading: Reptiles (turtles especially):
chunks.text: - A found turtle: determine pet vs native/wild before acting. A pet red-eared slider needs rehoming (NYTTS, Earthlings NYC); a native wild turtle should generally be left where found or, if injured, taken to a wild-turtle rehabber (NYTTS / Lorri Cramer). Never relocate a healthy native turtle far from where it was found.

chunks.heading: General:
chunks.text:
- Animal Care Centers of NYC (nycacc.org) handles lost-and-found for animals it takes in across all five boroughs and is the citywide safety net for found exotics you cannot place.
- Whatever the species: photograph the animal, note the exact found location, post to species-specific groups, and contact the relevant rescue in the main directory promptly.

guides.title: Boarding, pet sitting and planning ahead
guides.summary: Care while you are away, and arranging for a pet to be looked after if you no longer can.

chunks.heading: Boarding, pet sitting and planning ahead
chunks.text:
_Care while you are away, and arranging for a pet to be looked after if you no longer can._

> Boarding, sitting, grooming, life-planning & health alerts (exotic-specific unmet needs)

This tab covers needs that don't fit a rescue directory but come up constantly for exotic owners in NYC - and that ordinary kennels, pet-sitters and cat/dog resources usually can't meet. Confirm each provider still serves your species and check current requirements (most require a recent exotic-vet exam) before booking.

chunks.heading: EXOTIC BOARDING & PET-SITTING (most dog/cat kennels will NOT take exotics; these specialize):
chunks.text:
- AMC and The Center for Avian & Exotic Medicine (see the Exotic-vet tab) and other exotic vets often offer MEDICAL boarding - the safest option for a bird/reptile/small mammal with health needs, since a vet is on site.
- Long Island Bird & Exotics Vet Clinic (Nassau County; serves all NYC) - medical boarding for birds, reptiles, small mammals and small marsupials in an exotics-only facility (no dogs/cats to stress them); birdexoticsvet.com.
- Andrew Perrin Animal Services (Manhattan, 10022) - specialized reptile & exotic boarding/care; andrewperrinanimalservices.com.
- Bird Girl Pet Services (Hicksville, NY) - in-home parrot/reptile/small-mammal boarding with species-appropriate heat/UVB/misting and strict disease protocols (requires an annual exotics-vet wellness exam; note RHDV2 precautions for rabbits); birdgirlpetservices.com. (Does not board ferrets or animals illegal to own locally.)
- FSALT Pampered Exotic Pet Boarding (Hudson Valley - Dutchess/Putnam/Westchester/Orange/Ulster) - run by a licensed vet professional; boards buns, chinchillas, guinea pigs, hedgehogs, sugar gliders, ferrets, birds and reptiles, incl. medical boarding; fsaltpb.com.
- Long Island Parrot Society keeps a member-vetted PET-SITTER and GROOMER list (liparrots.org/pet-sitter, /groomers) - useful for finding a bird-experienced sitter in the NYC/LI area.
- Always ask a sitter/boarder: do you have exotic-vet experience with my species, what's your emergency vet, and how do you handle heat/UVB/power outages? A generator or climate backup matters for reptiles and birds.

chunks.heading: EXOTIC GROOMING (nail/beak/wing trims, shell/tooth checks - do NOT DIY a beak or a rabbit's teeth):
chunks.text:
- Exotic vets (AMC, Center for Avian & Exotic Medicine, Long Island Bird & Exotics) do nail/beak/wing trims and dental checks safely - a slipped beak or wing trim can injure a bird, so use a professional.
- LIPS groomer list (liparrots.org/groomers) for bird-specific grooming in the NYC/LI area.
- Rabbit and guinea-pig nail trims and dental exams: the rabbit rescues in the main directory and rabbit-savvy vets; overgrown rabbit teeth are a medical emergency, not a grooming task.

chunks.heading: LIFE-PLANNING: who cares for your exotic if you can't? (critical for long-lived species)
chunks.text:
- Parrots can live 30-80+ years and routinely OUTLIVE their owners - the single biggest reason big parrots cycle through many homes. Name a caregiver and put your bird in your estate plan. A pet TRUST (recognized in NY) funds and directs care without waiting for probate; a will alone can leave a bird in limbo. Specify the caregiver, a backup, and funds for food/vet care. Discuss it with the caregiver in advance.
- Long-lived tortoises (some 50-100+ yrs) need the same planning; even rabbits/parrots of 10-15 yrs warrant a named backup caregiver.
- Rescues that promise lifetime sanctuary for non-placeable animals (e.g. Woodstock/Catskill for farmed animals; parrot rescues that take returns) can be named as a fallback - confirm with them first and note it in your plan.
- Consult an estate attorney about a NY pet trust; many will add a companion-animal provision to a standard will.

chunks.heading: DISASTER / EVACUATION PLANNING (exotics need species-specific prep that generic plans miss):
chunks.text:
- Keep a species-ready GO-KIT: a secure travel carrier/cage, a portable heat source + battery pack (reptiles/birds can't survive a cold apartment in a winter outage), bottled water, several days of the exact food/hay, meds, and copies of vet records + your exotic vet's after-hours number.
- Birds are extremely sensitive to smoke, fumes and temperature swings; reptiles depend on heat/UVB; rabbits overheat fast. Plan for power loss and for a place that will take exotics (many human shelters and even pet shelters won't).
- Microchip/band and photograph each animal now (see the Lost-found & ID tab) so you can prove ownership and reunite after an evacuation. NYC emergency info: nyc.gov/emergencymanagement (search 'pets').

chunks.heading: SPECIES HEALTH ALERTS (current, NYC-relevant - these change; verify the latest before acting):
chunks.text:
- RABBITS - RHDV2 (Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus 2): highly contagious, usually fatal, and detected in domestic rabbits in NYC in 2020. Spreads via rabbit-to-rabbit contact AND contaminated food, bedding, clothing, shoes. A US-authorized VACCINE now exists - ask a rabbit-savvy vet about vaccinating. Basic biosecurity: wash hands before/after handling, don't bring in rabbits/products from unknown sources, keep house-rabbits away from wild rabbits. NYS info: dec.ny.gov (RHDV2); AMC RHDV2 guide: amcny.org.
- BIRDS - Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI/'bird flu'): widespread in NY wild birds and poultry (70+ NY flocks since 2022; still active in 2026). Public risk is low, but protect pet/backyard birds: keep them away from wild ducks/geese and their droppings, limit outdoor access, and practice biosecurity. Do NOT handle sick/dead wild birds yourself - report wild-bird die-offs to NYS DEC (dec.ny.gov, HPAI reporting); poultry concerns to NYS Ag & Markets (agriculture.ny.gov/hpai). Wildlife rehabbers cannot treat HPAI - never bring a sick wild bird into a home with pet birds.
- RabbitS/reptiles/birds generally - QUARANTINE any new exotic away from your existing animals for several weeks and get an exotics-vet exam before introducing them; many exotic diseases are silent carriers.
